items: Forms during high-temperature cooking. High doses caused cancer in laboratory animals. Those doses were much greater than the levels in food. All 29 restaurant french-fry samples in this table had acrylamide. The median of all 29 was 270 µg/kg, and the range was 117 to 1,030. Fuddruckers is not on this map. Its two samples were 346 and 452. A later FDA table, data through October 7, 2004, reports single samples: McDonald's french fries 428, Chick-fil-A waffle fries 271, Long John Silver's french fries 337, Burger King hash browns 768, Taco Bell Mexican pizza 53, and a Taco Bell bean burrito below the detection limit. Acrylamide forms when sugars and the amino acid asparagine are cooked at high temperature, as in frying. The FDA reports that high levels caused cancer in laboratory animals, and that those levels were much greater than the levels in human food. The map shows the chains in the 2002 fry table that are on this map. The marks are every tagged location, not the restaurants the FDA sampled.

Aggression and irritability These studies asked whether a food chemical is associated with aggression. Evidence that one chemical causes aggression in people is limited. A study of hyperactivity or irritability is not a study of aggression. None of these studies tested the restaurants drawn on the map. Of these, the trans fat study is the one that measured aggression in adults. The color and preservative studies are about hyperactivity, irritability, or attention. The soft-drink study counts fights and does not name a chemical.

Artificial food colors and sodium benzoate

McCann and coauthors, 2007, gave 153 children age 3 and 144 children age 8 or 9 a drink. The drink contained a mixture of artificial colors and sodium benzoate, or a placebo. Some mixtures were followed by higher hyperactivity scores. The Lancet. The outcome was hyperactivity, not aggression. Each drink mixed several additives, so the trial does not say which additive produced the change. The European Food Safety Authority later called the evidence limited. The effect was small, it was not consistent across ages and mixtures, and the authority did not change the safety evaluation of those additives. EFSA.

Blue slips A blue slip is the paper the Senate Judiciary Committee sends to the two senators from a nominee's home state. The president nominates the judge. Those senators return the paper if they will let the committee take up that nomination. For a district court, the committee does not hold a hearing unless both senators return the slip. A circuit nomination can be heard without the slips. The committee does not publish each paper. A hearing, a place on the Executive Calendar, or a confirmation is the public sign that both district-court slips came back. Blue is this paper only. It is not a party, and it is not a yes or a no.

Dengate and Ruben, 2002, gave 27 children bread with calcium propionate or a placebo. The children had already been selected because their behavior improved on a diet that removed additives. Average behavior scores were not significantly different. Relative to placebo, behavior worsened for 52% and improved for 19%. PubMed. The group was small and already selected. The authors describe irritability, restlessness, inattention, and sleep disturbance in some children. The paper does not report a finding on aggression.

Chemicals measured These are not the only chemicals that can be in fast food. Each group is one published study. A percent in one group is not comparable to a percent in another. Edwards and coauthors bought 64 foods in San Antonio in 2017 and 2018 and measured 11 plasticizers. A hamburger with toppings had cheese, tomato, pickles, onion, lettuce, and condiments. A plain patty had none of those. Chicken burritos were ordered two ways: white rice, black beans, cheese, mild salsa, and lettuce; or refried pinto beans, cheese, onion, sour cream, tomato, lettuce, and a tomato sauce. violent property murder robbery assault burglary fbi Crime These are the FBI's numbers for 2025. The map opens on fraud arrests from Table 69: arrests by state for agencies that sent 12 months of data. Orange is a Table 69 arrest rate. Indigo is an estimated offense rate, offenses known to law enforcement. The rate is the count divided by the population for that state, times 100,000. On an orange map, that population is the one printed for the state in Table 69. On an indigo map, it is the population printed on the FBI's offense row. On a neighborhood map, a city population of a few hundred people can produce a high rate from a small count. Violent crime is murder and nonnegligent manslaughter, rape, robbery, and aggravated assault. Property crime is burglary, larceny-theft, and motor vehicle theft. Arson has no estimate in this file. Fraud, forgery and counterfeiting, and embezzlement are the first measures. Where an agency sent 3 to 11 months, the FBI estimated the missing months from that agency's reports. Where an agency sent fewer than 3 months, the FBI estimated from similar places in the state. The FBI's summary of this release says estimated violent crime fell 9.3 percent from 2024 to 2025, and estimated property crime fell 12.4 percent. It says 17,075 agencies sent data, covering 96.2 percent of the population, and that the figures are as of April 2, 2026. The 2024 figures in the file were updated for this release. The file notes that limited data for 2025 were available for Florida and North Dakota. The District of Columbia row includes offenses reported by the Metro Transit Police and the District of Columbia Fire and Emergency Medical Services Arson Investigation Unit.

High doses in rats reduced litter size and the weight of the offspring. The highest amount was in chicken burritos: median 45.7 µg/kg, against 6.7 in hamburgers with toppings. It was not detected in cheese pizza, chicken nuggets, or plain patties. One Tex-Mex chain's foods had a median of 63.4 µg/kg. The other was below the detection limit. The paper does not say which chain was which. DEHA is an adipate, not a phthalate. In rats, a high dose reduced litter size and the weight of the offspring. The same reviews did not find the drop in testosterone seen with DEHP. The Tex-Mex chains in the study were Taco Bell and Chipotle.

Lower testosterone, lower sperm motility, and preterm birth. DEHP was in every hamburger with toppings. The hamburger median was 36 µg/kg. Chicken nuggets were 26, fries 23.7, chicken burritos 23, and plain patties 14. It was not detected in cheese pizza. Across all foods from one hamburger chain the median was 44 µg/kg, and from the other it was 23. The paper does not say which chain was higher. ATSDR reports that higher exposure in men has been linked with lower testosterone and lower sperm motility. Higher exposure in pregnancy has been linked with preterm birth and, in children, with a shift in the timing of puberty and with testicles that do not descend. In animals it damages the testes and, before birth, male reproductive development. The EPA review called the human evidence for those male reproductive effects robust. The hamburger chains in the study were McDonald's and Burger King.

Harm of the DEHP kind is not established. The highest amount was in chicken burritos: median 6,000 µg/kg in the 6 burritos tested for DEHT. Hamburgers with toppings were 2,200 µg/kg. None of the 3 orders of french fries had it. Cheese pizza, chicken nuggets, and plain patties were not tested for DEHT. DEHT is a terephthalate used in place of DEHP. In the animal studies the Consumer Product Safety Commission reviewed, it did not reduce fertility or sperm measures. The fast-food paper says most of those studies were paid for by industry, and that the few human studies of hormones do not agree. Harm of the kind shown for DEHP is not established. Those burritos were bought at Taco Bell and Chipotle. The paper does not say which of the two had more.

Linked with preterm birth. Evidence of male reproductive effects is slight. The only median above the detection limit was in plain hamburger patties: 16.5 µg/kg, and all 4 patties had it. DEP was also found in 5 of 10 orders of fries and 8 of 21 hamburgers with toppings, but those medians were below the detection limit. DEP is a weaker suppressor of testosterone than DEHP or DnBP in animal studies. The EPA review found slight evidence of male reproductive effects in people, and moderate evidence of a link with preterm birth. The patties came from the hamburger chains in the study, McDonald's and Burger King. The paper does not say which chain's patties were higher.

Can suppress testosterone in animals. Evidence in people is slight. DiBP was measured only in the first round. The highest median was in hamburgers with toppings: 2.7 µg/kg, in 7 of 8 hamburgers. Cheese pizza was 1.9 and fries were 1.2. Chicken nuggets and plain patties were below the detection limit. DiBP is close in structure to DnBP, and in animals it can suppress testosterone. The EPA review found only slight evidence in people. It said the studies were fewer, and the exposures lower, than for DnBP. The hamburger chains in the study were McDonald's and Burger King. The paper does not give a named-chain ranking for DiBP.

Higher liver and kidney weights in the parent animals. That study found no effect on reproduction. The only median above the detection limit was in plain hamburger patties: 16.3 µg/kg, in 2 of 4 patties. In hamburgers with toppings the median was below the detection limit, and the 95th percentile was 590 µg/kg. It was not detected in fries, chicken burritos, or cheese pizza. The paper found DINCH in hamburgers from only one of the two hamburger chains, and does not name that chain. DINCH is a replacement plasticizer. A two-generation study in rats found no effect on reproduction at doses up to 1,000 mg per kilogram of body weight a day. The parent animals had higher liver and kidney weights. The fast-food paper says later experiments disagree about the testes, and human studies are few. The hamburger chains in the study were McDonald's and Burger King.

Linked with lower testosterone and changes in semen measures. DiNP was measured only in the first round. It was in every chicken burrito, median 36 µg/kg. Cheese pizza was 5.9. It was not detected in hamburgers, fries, chicken nuggets, or plain patties. One Tex-Mex chain's median was 53 µg/kg and the other's was 11.5. The paper does not say which chain was higher. The EPA review found moderate evidence linking DiNP with lower testosterone and changes in semen measures. That evidence is weaker than the evidence for DEHP. The Tex-Mex chains in the study were Taco Bell and Chipotle.

Distribution centers Martin Brower publishes street addresses for distribution centers that supply McDonald's restaurants. Those addresses are geocoded and drawn with a factory mark. The list does not say where the food is manufactured, and it does not give the roads between a center and a restaurant. No line on this map is a delivery route.

Not detected. Not established as a testosterone suppressor. DMP was not detected in any of the 64 foods. DMP was not detected in any food in this study. It is a smaller phthalate, and it is not established as a testosterone suppressor the way DEHP is. There is no chain to rank, because the chemical was not found.

Can suppress testosterone. Linked with semen measures and a longer time to pregnancy. DnBP was in every hamburger with toppings and every cheese pizza. The medians were close: 4.8 µg/kg in hamburgers, 4.5 in fries, 4.1 in cheese pizza, 3.5 in chicken burritos, and 2.4 in chicken nuggets. The paper says the food medians were statistically similar. Across all foods from one hamburger chain the median was 5.0 µg/kg, and from the other it was 2.8. The paper does not say which chain was higher. DnBP can suppress testosterone. An EPA review of human studies found robust evidence linking it with semen measures and a longer time to pregnancy. In animals it disrupts development of the male reproductive system. The hamburger chains in the study were McDonald's and Burger King.

Animal studies report changes in the liver. DnOP was uncommon. It was detected in 3 of 8 cheese pizzas and 1 of 7 orders of chicken nuggets, and every median was below the detection limit. One pizza chain's foods had a median of 2.3 µg/kg. The other pizza chain was below the detection limit. The paper does not say which chain was which. DnOP was outside the EPA review of reproductive effects. Animal studies report changes in the liver. Evidence that it suppresses testosterone the way DEHP does is limited. The pizza chains in the study were Pizza Hut and Domino's.

EPA recorded an E. coli maximum contaminant level violation under the Revised Total Coliform Rule. Fecal coliform and E. coli indicate that the water may be contaminated with human or animal wastes. Disease-causing microbes in these wastes can cause diarrhea, cramps, nausea, headaches, or other symptoms. These pathogens may pose a special health risk for infants, young children, and people with severely compromised immune systems.

A marker for PFAS in packaging, not a measurement of the food. Some PFAS are associated with cancer, developmental toxicity, and immunotoxicity. Of 407 packages, 33% had detectable total fluorine. Dessert and bread wrappers and Tex-Mex packaging had higher detection rates than the other food-contact papers. The main table does not name the chains. A subset of 20 packages was tested for individual PFAS. Some samples with high total fluorine did not show high levels of the PFAS that test could measure. The study measured total fluorine in packaging as a marker for PFAS, which are per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances. The authors write that some PFAS have been associated with cancer, developmental toxicity, immunotoxicity, and other health effects. This chart is not a measurement of those effects in a person, and it is not a measurement of the food. The map is not filtered. The published detection table does not name the restaurants.

Leaders.vote · This week’s letter From the publisher · November 10, 2026 · 9 min read The Price of Competition: Who Is Being Left Out of the World’s Highest-Paying Esports Tournaments? An investigation into prize money, restricted participation, geographic representation, human genetic recycling, and rhythm entrainment in competitive gaming. Leaders.vote · November 10, 2026 Competitive gaming has developed into an international industry where professional players and organizations compete for millions of dollars in prize money. In 2026, the Esports World Cup announced a total prize pool of $75 million. Fortnite’s Global Championship offered $400,000 to its winning duo, while the Rocket League World Championship offered $300,000 to its winning team. $75 million Esports World Cup, 2026, the whole event $7 million to the winning Club Championship organization $400,000 Fortnite’s winning duo $300,000 Rocket League’s winning team $500,000 EVO Las Vegas, across twelve fighting games These competitions operate through different qualification systems, regional allocations, and organizational requirements. Some allow independent competitors to enter open qualifiers. Others require participation through designated professional leagues or established competitive organizations. I’m examining whether the world’s highest-paying esports competitions disproportionately restrict opportunities for players from countries and populations where rhythm entrainment may contribute to competitive performance. My research uses fighting games, multiplayer online battle arenas (MOBAs), first-person shooters (FPS), and MMORPG player-versus-player (PvP) combat to examine relationships between rhythmic synchronization, temporal prediction, pattern recognition, motor coordination, and player performance. My observations have led me to investigate whether players demonstrating stronger rhythmic synchronization consistently outperform those who demonstrate less of it. I’m comparing those observations with the geographic distribution of international esports opportunities, particularly in competitions offering substantial financial rewards. I’m also investigating whether game publishers have identified relevant performance patterns through their behavioral data and whether those findings, if they exist, have influenced tournament structures. The financial rewards available through esports vary considerably, as do the qualification systems governing access to them. The 2026 Esports World Cup announced a $75 million prize pool across 25 tournaments, individual awards, and its cross-game Club Championship. Of that amount, $30 million was allocated to the Club Championship, with $7 million designated for the winning organization. More than $39 million was allocated across individual game championships. The Fortnite Global Championship featured a $2 million prize pool, with $400,000 designated for the winning duo, or $200,000 per player. The Rocket League World Championship featured a $1.2 million prize pool, with $300,000 designated for the winning team. By comparison, EVO Las Vegas 2026 distributed $500,000 across twelve fighting-game tournaments, with first-place payouts in the tens of thousands of dollars. These amounts represent different types of financial awards. The Esports World Cup total covers an entire multi-game event, Fortnite’s and Rocket League’s figures refer to individual championships, and EVO’s total covers twelve separate tournaments. The participation systems also differ. EVO allows eligible players to register directly for its open-bracket competitions without professional team contracts. Fortnite and Rocket League provide open qualification pathways, subject to eligibility and regional requirements. League of Legends Worlds, by contrast, requires teams to advance through designated professional competitive systems. The Esports World Cup combines multiple qualification structures across its participating games, including established professional circuits, regional qualifiers, and other publisher-approved pathways. I’m examining whether larger financial rewards are associated with more restrictive participation systems, how those restrictions vary geographically, and which populations have access to the qualification process. The comparison also considers how much prize money reaches individual competitors, how much is awarded to organizations, and whether independent players have opportunities to compete for those rewards. International esports competitions do not provide identical qualification opportunities to every country. Some regions receive more championship places, professional infrastructure, and investment than others. The 2026 Esports Nations Cup’s Counter-Strike 2 qualification structure, for example, allocated four regional championship places each to Western and Eastern Europe, compared with one each for North Africa and Sub-Saharan Africa. These allocations establish differences in championship representation. They do not, by themselves, establish discriminatory intent or differences in competitive ability. I’m comparing tournament structures with the geographic distribution of players, regional qualification opportunities, competitive results, and available infrastructure. The investigation also examines whether competitors from countries with limited representation have opportunities to demonstrate their abilities before championship allocations are determined. A country may have an active gaming population without possessing the professional infrastructure, tournament partnerships, or regional qualification pathways required to participate in certain international competitions. This creates a distinction between access to a video game and access to its professional competitive ecosystem. My research uses fighting games, MOBAs, FPS, and MMORPG PvP environments to examine relationships between rhythmic synchronization, temporal prediction, motor coordination, and competitive performance. Rhythm entrainment involves synchronizing behavior with an external rhythmic signal. Different game genres provide opportunities to observe these functions under different conditions. Fighting games involve responding to attack patterns, movement sequences, and narrow timing windows. MOBAs involve coordinating abilities, movement, and team engagements around changing conditions. FPS environments involve movement timing, strafing, coordinated attacks, and anticipation of opponents’ actions. MMORPG PvP provides environments for examining movement synchronization, attack timing, opponent prediction, defensive responses, and adaptation to changing combat patterns. Duels, arenas, battlegrounds, and open-world PvP allow observations across different combat systems, including tab-targeting and action-oriented combat. MMORPG PvP also offers opportunities to observe how players adapt to opponents over repeated encounters, including changes in movement patterns, ability timing, and combat decisions. My observations suggest that players demonstrating stronger rhythmic abilities may possess competitive advantages in certain situations. I’m investigating whether these observations can be reproduced through controlled measurements and whether the relationship remains after accounting for experience, practice, equipment, and other factors. Precise timing, temporal prediction, and rhythm entrainment are related but distinct functions. Gameplay performance alone does not establish which function accounts for a particular result. I’m also examining whether geographic differences in tournament participation overlap with independently measured differences in rhythm-related performance. epa drinking water violation Water These are active community water systems in EPA's Drinking Water System Search. A community system serves homes. The number is EPA's count of quarters with a Safe Drinking Water Act violation over the past three years. That count includes monitoring and reporting violations. It is not a measurement from one tap, and it is not a score this page calculated. A health-based flag means EPA currently marks a violation of a maximum contaminant level, a maximum residual disinfectant level, or a treatment technique. Neighborhoods use the same OpenStreetMap names as the restaurant list. A neighborhood is matched to the community system that serves the most people among systems whose served city matches that neighborhood's city and state. A neighborhood with no matching served city is not drawn. EPA does not publish a separate result for the neighborhood. Roads and cities: OpenFreeMap, OpenMapTiles, OpenStreetMap. Each block is one quarter in this count, up to 12. Cyan fills one block for each quarter with a violation. A chemical appears here when EPA names it on a current health-based violation. Current means the violation is unaddressed or addressed in the 2026Q3 snapshot. Resolved and archived violations are not listed. Above a limit means a maximum contaminant level: EPA recorded that contaminant above the allowed amount. A missed test is not included. A treatment technique is a required process, not a chemical measured in the water. EPA does not publish a ranking of which contaminant is most harmful, and this page does not calculate one. Health goal of zero means EPA's public-health goal is no amount of that contaminant. The sentence is EPA's description of exposure above the limit, from the National Primary Drinking Water Regulations.

Economist running for governor of Vermont. Her campaign says she was born and raised in rural Vermont and has spent her career helping governments build economies that work for people. She says strong communities are built by neighbors, not by distant institutions. She proposes free universal primary and preventive care, with a community doctor for every Vermonter. She wants permanently affordable housing paid for in part by taxes on private equity, second homes, and luxury estates, and she wants to ban AI data centers. She says the state should invest in local businesses, farmers, workers, and cooperatives so more wealth stays in Vermont.
Secretary of State · New Mexico · Democratic

Doña Ana County clerk running for secretary of state. Amanda López Askin says she is in her second term as clerk of Doña Ana County, grew up in Las Cruces, and previously worked as a family and mental health therapist. She says she is running to protect the right to vote and to keep elections safe, secure, and fair. She says the office should make campaign finance more transparent. She says she would give small businesses clearer, more stable dealings with the state.

Yakima County commissioner running for Congress. She says she came from a family rooted in faith, agriculture, and service, worked in banking, and has used county office to challenge COVID rules, secure water, and flag fraud. She says government should protect people and leave decisions with those closest to the consequences. She says she will stand with President Trump on the border, energy production, constitutional rights, and federal spending. Her stated priorities are faith, family, agriculture, public safety, and freedom for central Washington.

Registered nurse running for Congress The campaign says Amanda Pusczek is a registered nurse who has spent more than a decade on double shifts and disaster work, and that she is running because rural hospitals, public schools, and family farms in north Alabama have been squeezed. She says she is not a millionaire and will not take corporate PAC money. She says rural hospital closures and cuts to safety-net programs have left medical gaps, and she wants federal help to keep emergency rooms and maternity care open. She supports a $15 federal minimum wage, stronger union rights, and antitrust rules aimed at meatpacking and other concentrated industries. She wants family farmers protected from what she calls a poultry tournament system, plus a federal right to repair farm equipment.

Physician and U.S. representative running in a new district. He says every American should have affordable coverage, and he opposes turning Medicare into a voucher system. He says he would cut waste and fraud, strengthen the doctor-patient relationship, and invest in research including stem cell research. He says rural and mountain communities need primary care, telehealth, broadband, and stable funding for rural hospitals and clinics.

Emergency physician and former state representative running for Congress in Arizona's 1st District. His campaign says he is an emergency doctor who won three terms in the Arizona House and had more bills signed than any Democrat in the legislature over the last decade. He says that work focused on teacher pay, small businesses, and public health. He says he would roll back tariffs he calls a tax on groceries and gas, and protect Social Security, Medicare, and Medicaid. He says only a woman and her doctor should make reproductive decisions, and he wants abortion rights written into federal law. He says he would reduce gun violence, fund police, stop fentanyl, and fight for Arizona's share of Colorado River water.

Educator and entrepreneur running for Congress The campaign says Ammie Akin is an educator and entrepreneur who has taught students with disabilities, trained school leaders, and with her husband is turning a former elementary school into a shared campus for nonprofits. She says she is ready to represent Alabama's 7th District. She says she will put families, workers, small businesses, and local communities ahead of party politics and will fight wasteful federal spending. She wants rural hospitals kept open and health care that does not depend on how far a family lives from a provider. She says schools should be a partnership among teachers, parents, and the community, and that students should be prepared for college or a career.

Physician running for governor. Her campaign says she grew up in Youngstown under difficult circumstances and is a doctor, advocate, and problem-solver. She says she is running because families are struggling while wealthy interests pull the state in another direction. The site lists lower household costs, health-care costs, education, jobs, worker protections, safer communities, and corruption as her priorities. A campaign update says medical debt should be eliminated and health care made more affordable. She also lists reproductive freedom and the ability to age in place among the issues on the site.

Physician running for Congress The campaign says Dr. Amy Chai is a primary-care and addiction physician running for Connecticut's 1st District. She describes growing up in extreme poverty, training at Johns Hopkins, Indiana University, Michigan, and Virginia, and later being named a U.S. Presidential Teacher. She says the middle class is struggling and that she wants local economies, small businesses, and American industry strengthened so people can afford a home and a family. Her issues page also focuses on health care, mental health and addiction, education and parents' rights, and taxes. She says government spending and legislation should be easier for the public to see.

U.S. senator and former Hennepin County attorney. Her campaign says she led Hennepin County's prosecutor's office for eight years and has served in the Senate, where she highlights bipartisan bills and a law letting Medicare negotiate drug prices. She is running for governor and says she wants state government to be more accountable. She says she would work to lower health care, housing, child care, and utility bills, and to build more homes. She says she would root out fraud and make it easier to start a business and get a permit. She says she would take on organized crime and gang violence and help local police hire and keep officers.

U.S. representative and former union organizer for New Jersey's 11th District. She says she led New Jersey Working Families, directed politics for Bernie Sanders's 2020 campaign, and served in the Labor Department. She says she has spent 25 years fighting for working families, including New Jersey's $15 minimum wage and paid sick days. Attorney general of Massachusetts, running for re-election. Andrea Campbell's site says she was born and raised in Roxbury and the South End, went from foster care to Princeton and into public service, and is the first Black woman to serve as the state's attorney general. She says she is trying to make life more affordable by putting money back into people's pockets. She says she is defending freedoms against rollbacks from the Trump era. She says she is fighting for the next generation and for wider opportunity for every child, including reproductive rights, civil rights, and cases against powerful corporations.

Independent candidate for governor. Andrea James's site says her family has lived in Massachusetts for seven generations and that she is running to put the government's agenda on the needs of people. She says a governor's priorities should be housing, health care, child care, education, and quality of life, and she calls housing a human right. She says people should be able to see a doctor without going into debt and that families should have child care they trust. She says Massachusetts should not have contracts with ICE, and she wants data centers banned in favor of lower utility costs and green energy.

U.S. representative for Oregon's 6th District, seeking another term. Her campaign says her father immigrated from Mexico, served in the military, and spent three decades as a police officer, and that she was the first in her family to finish college. It says she worked in the Oregon Legislature on health care, the minimum wage, and paid family leave before her election to Congress. She says she will fight rising costs for working families, seek more living-wage jobs, and keep backing worker protections and investments in rural health care, education, and infrastructure. She says she led efforts to cap prescription prices in Oregon and is pushing Congress to let Medicare negotiate drug prices and to strengthen hospital and insurance price transparency. She also treats mental health and substance use as part of health care that is too often overlooked.

Health-care and business candidate running for Congress in Wisconsin's 5th District. His campaign says he is the son of Wisconsin's union movement, a product of public schools, and not a career politician. It says he built a career in health care and business beside workers and manufacturers. He says he would bring practical leadership aimed at lower costs, good-paying jobs, and better health care. He says protecting fair elections and democratic institutions is the issue that makes progress on jobs, health care, and education possible. He says women must be able to make their own reproductive-health decisions and that Congress should secure that right.

U.S. representative, Navy veteran, and firearms-business owner. He says he was commissioned from Notre Dame, served 28 years in the Navy including three combat deployments to Kuwait and Iraq, then earned a master's from the University of Georgia and built Clyde Armory from a garage hobby into a company with two Georgia stores. Elected in 2020, he says he serves on the Appropriations and Budget committees. He says that on April 12, 2013, the IRS confiscated $940,000 from his business through civil asset forfeiture, and that the agency later offered to return part of it if he forfeited the rest. He says most small-business owners hit by that process lacked the money to fight, and he presents the case as a fight against overreaching government. On guns, he argues that taxes on firearms and ammunition, from the National Firearms Act to local per-gun taxes, treat a constitutional right as a privilege and could tax it out of reach.

U.S. representative for New York's 2nd District. His campaign says he has represented the district since 2021 and chairs the House Homeland Security Committee. It also says he is vice chair of a Financial Services subcommittee on capital markets. He says he led the push for permanent funding of the World Trade Center Health Program. He says a tax law he supported raised the state-and-local tax deduction cap from $10,000 to $40,000 and ended federal tax on tips. Independent candidate for the U.S. Senate. He says candidates, including himself, have a duty to serve the public rather than foreign governments or corporations.

Small-business owner and plumber running for Congress The campaign says Andrew Sneed was born and raised in Huntsville, graduated from Lee High, and later left restaurant work to start over as a plumber's helper. U.S. representative for Indianapolis and a former law enforcement officer. He says he hosts an annual job fair and a youth opportunities fair. He says he would invest in early childhood and K-12 schools, raise teacher pay, and expand Pell Grants and workforce training as alternatives to a four-year degree. He says tariffs are raising household costs, and he wants tax cuts for working families, small businesses, and entrepreneurs rather than policy aimed at the ultra-wealthy. He says he opposes cuts to SNAP, introduced a Food Deserts Act to finance grocery stores in underserved areas, and supports military and humanitarian aid to Ukraine.

U.S. representative from Kentucky running for the Senate. Andy Barr's campaign calls him an eighth-generation Kentuckian and says he was the first member of the state's House delegation to endorse Donald Trump and chaired Trump's 2024 Kentucky primary campaign. He says he would deport people he calls criminal illegal immigrants, restart border-wall construction, hire more border agents, restore Remain in Mexico, and end catch-and-release. He says he voted for tax cuts that end taxes on Social Security for seniors, on overtime, and on tips, and he wants to expand Kentucky coal and block climate rules he says were imposed through financial regulators. He says he will defend girls' sports and private spaces, veterans' disability and health benefits, the Second Amendment, police funding, sanctions on fentanyl tied to China, and Kentucky farmers, including a federal framework for hemp products.

U.S. representative Andy Biggs is an Arizona native who has represented the state's 5th Congressional District since 2016. He is running for governor with Sine Kerr for lieutenant governor. He says he will eliminate the state income tax, work with local governments to ease property taxes, and cut permitting barriers for new homes. He says he will end state incentives for data centers and set standards to protect Arizona's water and energy. He says he will reconvene a Border Strike Force aimed at human trafficking and drug trafficking and equip police to fight drug trafficking.

Green Party candidate for governor of Maryland. Andy Ellis says he has lived in Baltimore since 2005, coached debate, and spent nearly 15 years in corporate technology. He says he has spent more than a decade organizing the Green Party in Baltimore and across Maryland. He says the state should stop data-center projects that he argues threaten communities, water, and public health. He says unaffiliated and third-party voters are shut out of meaningful elections and that he has a plan aimed at two-party political corruption. He says the state should spread wealth, power, and opportunity so more residents have a say in incentives, public funds, and budgets.

Physician and U.S. representative who chairs the House Freedom Caucus. He chairs the Agriculture appropriations subcommittee. He says he is fighting to restore fiscal responsibility in Washington and protect taxpayer dollars. The campaign describes him as a common-sense conservative with the courage to change Washington. He says he is unafraid to speak for the priorities of Maryland's 1st District.

Community advocate running for Congress in Los Angeles. Angela Gonzales-Torres's campaign says she is a democratic socialist and a lifelong Angeleno from Highland Park, the daughter of a deportee who was raised by a single mother. She says she would abolish ICE, make Los Angeles more affordable, and increase access to critical services. She says housing, health care, and education should be affordable, and she wants higher taxes on the wealthy to pay for them. She says she would abolish super PACs so elections answer to voters rather than donors.

Entrepreneur running for Congress. Angela Rodriguez Prilliman's campaign says she is a Fort Worth mother and entrepreneur who grew up in Stephenville, graduated from Texas A&M, and spent more than a decade in technology. It says she is the Democratic candidate in the 12th District. She says she would seek universal health care and universal child care, paid for by taxes on billionaires. She also lists voting rights, full funding for public schools, and getting billionaire money out of politics. She says Congress should protect AI whistleblowers, set liability and testing rules, and restrict AI companions for children.

Florida state representative and union organizer She says she is a state representative, union organizer, and mother who was born and raised in Jacksonville. She says she supports free child care and pre-K, and a Working Families Guarantee for workers.

Neighborhood-council leader running for Congress. Angélica Dueñas's campaign says she was born in Sun Valley to parents who immigrated from Mexico, raised five children, and was the first in her family to finish college. She says she takes no corporate PAC, AIPAC, oil, or drug-company money, and she supports Medicare for All and housing as a right. She says she would abolish ICE, create a path to legal status, and pass the DREAM Act. She says she would raise the minimum wage, protect the right to unionize, and cancel student debt by making public college and trade school tuition-free.

U.S. representative for Missouri's 2nd District. She grew up working at her parents' carpet store in Manchester, studied business at the University of Missouri, and later held management jobs at Hallmark and Ralston Purina before coming to Congress. She says she has worked to cut taxes and regulation so local businesses can hire, and she voted for a tax bill that removes taxes on tips, overtime, and Social Security. She highlights the Fight Online Sex Trafficking Act and funding for rape-kit testing through the Debbie Smith Act. She says she will keep defending a right to life, and she introduced a bill to require medical care for infants born alive after an abortion.

Faith leader and small-business owner running for Congress in Tennessee's 3rd District. Her campaign says she is a progressive faith leader who owns Biased Apparel and is chief executive of Work of Place, a firm that helps congregations use their buildings for neighbors' economic stability. She and her husband Mike live in Chattanooga's Park Central neighborhood. She says workers deserve wages that cover the bills and the freedom to organize, and that rural counties need funded hospitals, schools, and infrastructure. She says she takes no corporate PAC money and wants fair elections and fair maps. She says she would protect reproductive freedom and LGBTQ+ people, treat health care as a human right, and fund Oak Ridge's science without sacrificing the land.

U.S. representative running for another term. Anna Paulina Luna's campaign says she is a mother, Air Force veteran, and one of the younger members of Congress who did not grow up with wealth or a political family. It says her father struggled with substance abuse and her mother raised her on her own. She says big government is often the problem, not the solution, and that her politics come from growing up in hard circumstances and serving in the military. She says she wants reforms aimed at problems people actually face rather than an elitist approach to Congress.

Former Wayland selectwoman and business executive running for secretary of state. Pediatrician running for U.S. Senate Annie Andrews's campaign says she is a pediatrician and mother who has cared for South Carolina children for nearly twenty years, from newborns to teenagers. She says she is not a career politician. She says families are struggling with grocery prices, child care, and the cost of health care, and her platform treats health care as a right. Her listed plans include tackling debt and congressional perks, cutting taxes, lowering premiums, protecting rural hospitals, and reversing Medicaid cuts. The platform also lists strong schools and affordable child care, reproductive freedom, political corruption, and an end to gun violence.

Libertarian candidate for lieutenant governor. He says he is a high school English and debate teacher in Cibolo and a military veteran. Republican candidate for New Hampshire's 1st District. His campaign says his great-grandparents came through Ellis Island and that he came to the University of New Hampshire in 1983. Former Macomb County clerk, running for Michigan secretary of state. Candidate for governor of Michigan. Anthony Hudson's campaign says he was born and raised in Texas and moved to Michigan in 2012 to be in his children's lives. He says he would stop data-center and solar-panel development and protect farmland. He says he wants lower taxes, smaller government, and decisions returned to local communities.

U.S. representative for Maryland's 6th District, seeking another term. Her campaign says she was raised in Buhl, Idaho, the daughter of a potato farmer, and is the mother of four. She points to her work expanding broadband and says technology should drive development across the 6th District. Attorney and former mayor running for Congress. April Verlato's campaign says she was born and raised in Arcadia, studied political science at UCLA, and earned a law degree at Southwestern. She says the economy should reward innovation and hard work rather than regulations she argues hold back workers and small businesses. She points to her role founding the Downtown Arcadia Improvement Association and says she focused on opportunities for minority-owned businesses. She says she would go to Congress to bring back good-paying jobs and economic growth.

Retired Navy captain running for Congress. Armen Kurdian's campaign says he is a retired Navy captain who served 25 years and is a husband, father, and neighbor in Southern California. He says California's utility bills are among the nation's highest and he would fight to make power cheaper and more reliable. He says he would bring back good-paying jobs, support small business, and cut regulations he argues are pushing employers out.

Libertarian candidate for railroad commissioner. He says he lives in Austin and has been a Libertarian activist for many years. He says mineral and surface owners should be protected from eminent-domain abuse, and that disputes with energy developers should be settled by voluntary agreements. Retired programmer and president of the Fairfax County Taxpayers Alliance. He says abortion takes a life, that it should stay legal in rare cases to save the mother, and that marriage should be encouraged. Clinician running for Congress in North Carolina's 10th District. U.S. representative from northeast Iowa running for the Senate. U.S. senator and former Florida attorney general She says she is a fifth-generation Floridian raised in Plant City who earned degrees from the University of Florida and a master of laws from Stetson. U.S. representative running for another term. Business owner running for Congress in Pennsylvania's 4th District. Aurora Stuski says she has lived in West Norriton for 35 years, owns a business, and is the mother of three. U.S. representative for Georgia's 8th District. He lives in Tifton and says his experience runs from the cattle farm to the boardroom. Elected to the Porter County Board of Commissioners in 2022, she says she knocked on more than 11,000 doors and has volunteered with Rotary and SCORE. She says safe cities, secure borders, and smarter spending are her vision, including arresting and prosecuting criminals and ending catch-and-release. She says she would curb inflation and waste so families keep more purchasing power, and reduce the national debt by putting American families and businesses ahead of foreign interests. She says schools should teach students how to think, that girls' sports and facilities should be reserved for biological females, and that law-abiding people should keep the right to bear arms.

Veterinarian running for Congress in Oregon's 1st District. Her campaign says Barbara Kahl is an Oregon native who spent about 20 years in business, including finance work at Intel, and earned her veterinary degree in 2006. It says she later served as chief veterinarian for American Samoa, where she built an animal-control unit, and that she has testified before the Oregon Legislature. She says economic growth comes first, through small-business relief, infrastructure, and jobs, and she wants housing built faster by cutting permitting delays. On schools, she supports public schools, school choice, vocational pathways, and funding that follows the student, and she says parents rather than federal officials should control curriculum. She also calls for lower health-care costs and stronger veterans' care, more accountable federal spending, forest stewardship that keeps timber communities working, and support for ports and local police.

Oakland mayor running for re-election. Barbara Lee says that in her year as mayor she has worked to root out corruption at City Hall, reopen fire stations, and stabilize the budget. She is asking voters for another four years. She says streets are getting cleaner and that she wants more good-paying local jobs. She says she will keep a broad approach to homelessness and add affordable housing across the city. She says she is using prevention programs against crime and wants Oakland to be a model of accountable city government.

U.S. representative and small-business owner Barry Moore is a member of Congress and the owner of a waste-removal and demolition company he and his wife started after he earned an agricultural science degree at Auburn and served in the Alabama National Guard. He previously served in the Alabama House, where he says he judged votes by faith, family, finance, and freedom. He says illegal immigration should face zero tolerance, and he wants people in the country illegally deported, beginning with those he calls the most violent. He points to tax cuts on tips, overtime, and Social Security, and says he is working to cut regulations and shrink the federal government. He says violent criminals should be prosecuted fully and that federal law enforcement should be funded to focus on crime rather than political opponents.

Marine infantry officer and attorney running for Indiana secretary of state. Beau Bayh's campaign describes him as a seventh-generation Hoosier who served as a Marine infantry officer and rose to captain, including the Scout Sniper Unit Leader's Course. He says his first priority is to stop waste and insider dealing in the secretary of state's office, including unnecessary travel, luxury vehicles, no-bid contracts, and high-paying jobs for family and friends. He says illegal votes should not count and that every eligible Hoosier should be able to vote. He supports statewide ballot referendums, including on redistricting, and says he will advocate for new small businesses and for working families.

U.S. representative for Vermont The campaign says Becca Balint is the first woman and openly LGBTQ+ person to represent Vermont in Congress. It says she is a teacher and parent, served in the state Senate, and now sits on the House Judiciary Committee and in the Progressive Caucus. Her campaign says housing is a human right and points to the Community Housing Act, which she introduced to fund affordable housing, renter protections, and down-payment help. The site says she has introduced bills to expand mental health care after disasters and for young people. It says she cosponsored the Freedom to Vote Act and the John Lewis Voting Rights Act and wants Supreme Court term limits and tighter ethics rules.

Democrat running for Congress in Nebraska's 3rd District. Her campaign says she is a lifelong resident of the 3rd District running against Adrian Smith, and that her neighbors include farmers, factory workers, and small-business owners facing the same pressures her family does. She says a nearby farm going to auction is part of why she is running. She says she would protect Social Security, Medicare, and SNAP, bring back funding Congress already approved, and invest in public schools without banning books. She supports unions, a woman's private medical decisions, veterans, and equipping police, and she says a secure border should come with a fair immigration system. She also says she would respect the Second Amendment while working to prevent violence, expand senior care, and improve access to health care.

Marine veteran running for Congress in Michigan's 2nd District. His campaign says he grew up on a farm in Hesperia, enlisted at 18, and served nearly 20 years in the Marine Corps as an infantryman, including combat tours. He says he is running to keep serving rural Michigan. He says he would bring down grocery and gas prices, back small businesses, strengthen collective bargaining, and bring manufacturing jobs back with Buy American policies. He supports more funding for public schools, larger Pell Grants, and vocational training, and he says he backs Medicare for All. He also lists veterans, the natural environment, and community safety among his priorities.

U.S. representative for Virginia's 6th District. Ben Cline's office says he serves on Judiciary, Appropriations, Intelligence, and Budget. He represented the 24th District in the Virginia House of Delegates from 2002 to 2018, chaired its Militia, Police, and Public Safety committee, and worked as an assistant commonwealth's attorney and as chief of staff to Congressman Bob Goodlatte. He grew up in Rockbridge County and lives in Botetourt County with his wife Elizabeth and their two daughters. His office lists the economy, energy, veterans, health care, and reforming Congress among the issues he works on.

Candidate for Congress who says Utah, not a party, will set his votes. He describes a childhood in which his mother worked as hard as anyone he knew, the lights sometimes went out, and he took his first job at 11. He says his work in Congress would focus on lowering housing costs, getting people medical care, and making daily life easier for Utah families. He says he will work with anyone for results and will also stand alone when he thinks democracy, protest, or due process is being trampled. His priorities page also lists protecting the environment and defending human rights and opportunity.

U.S. senator running for another term. Ben Ray Luján's campaign says he filed for another Senate term and has focused on costs, health care, and internet access for New Mexico. He says he has worked to lower prescription prices and to protect Medicare, Medicaid, and Social Security. He says he has defended nutrition assistance for working families, seniors, veterans, and rural communities. He says he has worked to connect families to the internet and to deliver results in all 33 counties.

U.S. representative for Mississippi's 2nd District. His campaign says he has a long record of bringing federal funding home, and that in 2024 and 2025 that work totaled nearly $4 billion. He won the 2026 Democratic nomination for the seat. The campaign says that funding covered health care, infrastructure, agriculture, and education. It also says the money covered broadband, public safety, clean water, and disaster recovery. He presents that record as results on the issues that matter most in the district.

Long-haul trucker and small-business owner running for Congress in Arizona's 8th District. Her campaign says she is a mother who grew up in a union family, earned a commercial driver's license in 1997, and logged more than 4 million miles over 27 years while running a small trucking business. She says a car accident ended an Army ROTC scholarship at the University of Arizona. She says she will lower the cost of groceries, fuel, and housing, protect Social Security and Medicare, and force drug companies to renegotiate prices. She says she will secure the border and stop trafficking, and support an earned path to citizenship for people who follow the law. She says she will fight lease-purchase deals that trap truck drivers in debt, defend the right to organize, and protect reproductive care and contraception.

Small-business owner Bernadette Wilson is a lifelong Alaskan who started a commercial waste company in 2016 and has led the Alaska Policy Forum and worked with Americans for Prosperity. She also served as a senior advisor on Nick Begich's congressional campaign. She says Alaska should move from talk to construction on projects including AKLNG, ANWR, Willow, the Ambler Road, and West Susitna access. She says she will restore the statutory Permanent Fund Dividend. She says Alaska's children should be able to attend strong schools in the state.

Retired Air Force lieutenant colonel running for Congress. Berney Flowers's site says he served nearly 21 years in the Air Force, with later work in national defense and cybersecurity, and that he was raised in a working-class family. He describes himself as a father, mentor, and veteran rather than a career politician. He says he advocates term limits, fiscal responsibility, and working across party lines. He says he supports taking politics out of public schools, parental involvement, and local control of education. He says he supports strong immigration enforcement, national defense, and public safety.

Retired Army major general and attorney running for the U.S. Senate. His campaign says he graduated first in his West Point class, earned a law degree from Harvard, and commanded troops in combat, including a joint task force in Afghanistan. It says he later held senior civilian posts in the Army and as an adviser at the CIA. He says he would focus on balancing the federal budget. He says he would lower the tax on selling a home and the broader tax burden on Virginia families. He says he would protect veterans' health benefits, ban members of Congress from trading stocks, and support new nuclear plants to bring down household energy costs.

Stay-at-home parent running for Congress in Pennsylvania's 13th District. Beth Farnham says she is a stay-at-home parent running again for the 13th District, with the support of her husband, Rob. She says she wants a representative who is accessible across the district. She says she would defend reproductive freedom, public education, gun safety, universal health care, and immigration reform. She also lists affordability and the environment, and says climate change requires action to protect agriculture and communities.

Author and former Roanoke Times reporter running for Congress. Her campaign says she grew up poor in a small Ohio town, was the first in her family to go to college, and spent 25 years at The Roanoke Times. She says her books include Factory Man, Dopesick, and Paper Girl, and that Dopesick became a Hulu series she helped produce. She says she is running to make life affordable for working families, expand health and mental health care, and invest in rural communities. She says every child should have a real chance by rebuilding the ladder that helped her leave poverty. She says she has stood with people overlooked by a system that benefits billionaires, including families hurt by addiction and workers whose jobs disappeared.

Former mayor running for Congress. Beth Van Duyne's campaign says she is a single working mother who left home at 17, put herself through college, and became the first woman mayor of her hometown before serving in a presidential administration. She says she is running in the 24th District so her children have the same opportunities she had, and she warns about socialism, the border, and hostile nations. She says she is a conservative who has fought government corruption, supported removing criminal noncitizens from North Texas, and backed growth and the Constitution.

Scientist and working mother running for Missouri's 3rd District. She grew up in Foristell, lives in St. Peters, and has worked as an environmental chemist testing crops and checking communities for lead and forever chemicals. She supports full, equal funding for public schools from pre-K through college and union apprenticeships. She wants affordable physical and mental health care, and federal infrastructure money for rural roads, bridges, broadband, and water. She ties her environmental work to clean air and water, and she supports the Women's Health Protection Act, the Equal Rights Amendment, and Medicare for All.

U.S. representative for Minnesota's 4th District. Betty McCollum's office says she has represented Saint Paul, Ramsey County, and most of Washington County since 2001, and that she was the second Minnesota woman elected to Congress since statehood. She serves as the top Democrat on the House Appropriations Defense Subcommittee. Her office says she champions education, environmental protection, health-care access and affordability, fiscal responsibility, and international engagement that pairs diplomacy and development with a strong national defense. She says she wants higher education kept affordable and public schools accountable to parents and local officials, and she supports universal health coverage and the Affordable Care Act. On defense, she says funding should keep the armed forces trained and equipped, with priority for military health care and ending military sexual assault.

U.S. senator running for re-election. He says he is a businessman and a former U.S. ambassador to Japan, and that serving Tennessee in the Senate has been the honor of his life. He says his business career shapes how he approaches the debates in the Senate. He says he is running to keep fighting for lower taxes, energy independence, secure borders, and the rule of law. He says his Senate work has included securing the southern border, supporting small businesses, and strengthening national security. He says he will keep pushing an America First agenda and treat the Chinese Communist Party as a serious adversary.

U.S. representative and small-business owner from Ottawa County. His campaign says he is a lifelong Ottawa County resident who built and ran a local business before Congress, and that he and his wife Natalie raised five children in southwest Michigan. He attended Holland Christian High School and earned a political science degree from Calvin College. He says he has pushed to rein in federal spending to fight inflation and lower the cost of energy, groceries, and housing. He supports more American energy production and fewer regulations so small businesses can hire. He says he backs limited government, secure borders, and safe communities, and that he has worked on Great Lakes and PFAS issues.

Former prosecutor and U.S. representative for southeastern Massachusetts. He says he was elected to the state House at 23, later served as a state senator and Norfolk district attorney, and won this U.S. House seat in 2010. He and his wife Tevis live in Bourne and have two adult children. He says he is challenging tariffs that raise prices and hurt small businesses, and that he wants health care that is more affordable and accessible. He says he has fought to protect Social Security, Medicare, reproductive rights, and veterans and military families. He says he serves on Foreign Affairs and Armed Services and has brought home federal money for coastal resiliency, public safety, clean energy, and jobs.
District 21 · U.S. House · New York · Democratic

Dairy farmer running for Congress in New York's 21st District. His campaign says his parents started a North Country dairy farm after the Peace Corps, and that he has run Twin Mill Farms with his wife and three sons for 22 years. It says he has also coached junior-varsity basketball, served on the Lisbon school board, and founded a nonprofit for children with cancer. He says he would repeal costly regulations, support fair trade, and bring manufacturing back so prices fall for families and for seniors on fixed incomes. He says this border district needs more Border Patrol staffing, a harder path for illegal entry and an easier legal one, and fixes to the guest-worker programs farms rely on. He says farms and Main Street businesses also need fewer burdensome rules and investment in rural roads and bridges.

Election-reform advocate running for U.S. Senate. Blake Huber says he has worked on campaigns since he was 17 and spent more than 30 years in management, including apartments, a small business, a motel, and teams of network engineers. He says he later chaired the Libertarian Party of Colorado, served on its national committee, and now focuses on how elections are run. He wants approval voting, so people can support every candidate they like and elections are not decided by fear of wasting a vote. He says immigration should pair orderly borders with a simpler legal path for people who pass background checks and want to work. He says federal rules bury small businesses in cost and paperwork, and that old rules should expire while new ones face a test of their economic impact.

State senator and oil-and-gas business owner running for Congress. A seventh-generation Louisianian and LSU graduate, he says he has owned a home in Baton Rouge for more than 25 years, expanded his family's oil and gas business, and is raising four children with his wife Ashley, a special-education teacher. He was elected to the state Senate in 2023. He says he passed a law so Louisiana can prosecute corrupt politicians after they leave office, and in Congress he would push term limits and a permanent ban on members trading individual stocks. He says he wrote the state law forcing New Orleans to follow immigration law, and he would finish a border wall, mandate E-Verify, and treat cartels as foreign terrorist organizations. He says he authored constitutional carry, banned Big Tech money in Louisiana elections, and banned ultra-processed food in school cafeterias.

U.S. representative for northern Utah. He says three terms in Congress have centered on costs, immigration, the military, and what he calls the Utah way of life, and he notes a constituent-service award for his office. He says he is pushing border security, American energy, fiscal discipline, and conservative social policy. He points to work strengthening Hill Air Force Base, expanding the charitable tax deduction, protecting the Great Salt Lake, and funding local water, roads, trails, and education.
