Candidate for railroad commissioner. He says he was raised in Midland by a father in the Texas energy business, entered the industry in 1994, and worked as an energy trader. He says he is also a rancher and mineral owner and has chaired the Tarrant County Republican Party. He says the Railroad Commission oversees oil and gas plus uranium, coal, and salt, and that the seat should be held by a conservative who will back the president. He says he will end diversity, equity, and inclusion programs, regulation he calls overbearing, and influence from radical Islam and the Chinese Communist Party in Texas oil. He says he will enforce the Legislature's ban on hostile foreign ownership of land in order to protect the Texas oil industry.

Union leader running for Congress in Pennsylvania's 7th District. Bob Brooks is a union president who says he has spent his career fighting for workers. He says he is running so Washington works for working people. He says that as a union president he pressed politicians for higher wages, better health care, and stronger benefits. His issues page lists affordability, health care, a higher minimum wage, stronger unions, housing costs, and ending corruption.

Former Navy submarine officer running for U.S. Senate. Bob Chew says he served as a Navy submarine officer during the Cold War and has spent three decades creating jobs. He says he is an independent candidate running for people who are tired of the two parties. He says he will measure success by problems solved and people helped, not by how much public money is spent. He says he cannot be bought or bullied, and that his promise is to Coloradans rather than to parties or donors.

Former teacher and Bucks County commissioner running for Congress in Pennsylvania's 1st District. Bob Harvie taught for 26 years before serving on the Bucks County Board of Commissioners. His campaign says he is running because working families are paying the price while Washington is in chaos. He says families deserve a fair shot to earn a living, afford a home, raise children, and retire with dignity. He describes the race as a chance to send someone to Congress who will fight for a better deal for working people.

Retired Air Force lieutenant colonel and former state senator running for secretary of state. His campaign says he is an Omaha native who served 21 years in the Air Force, including Desert Shield and Desert Storm and the Looking Glass mission at Offutt, and retired in 2000. It says Gov. Dave Heineman appointed him to the Legislature in 2009, voters reelected him, and colleagues chose him to chair the Executive Board. He says the secretary of state should run elections for every voter, make legal voting easy, make cheating difficult, and certify the results no matter who wins. He calls for public transparency, checks that safeguards against fraud are working, and support for the county officials who run elections. He says he would modernize the office where that improves service without weakening security, so people trust the count.

U.S. representative for Ohio's 5th District. His official biography says he has represented Ohio's 5th District since 2007 and is a senior member of the Energy and Commerce Committee, where he chairs the Energy Subcommittee. He says he has held more than 1,500 meetings in the district since 2012 and has had 35 bills and provisions signed into law. He lists rural broadband, less government spending, a strong national defense, the substance-use crisis, energy independence, and commonsense government reform as top priorities. He points to the INFO Act on opioid data, the Advanced Nuclear Technology Development Act, and the Critical Electric Infrastructure Act to protect the power grid. He highlights the Drinking Water Protection Act on algal toxins, faster processing of VA appeals, and laws on propane supply and precision-agriculture connectivity.

U.S. representative and physician from Missouri. His campaign describes a record in Congress and in Jefferson City centered on immigration enforcement, abortion limits, gun laws, and taxes. He highlights a bill aimed at visa overstays and earlier Missouri legislation against sanctuary cities and employment of people without legal status. He says he co-chairs the Pro-Life Caucus and has backed federal abortion limits, after authoring Missouri clinic rules and helping write the 2019 heartbeat bill. He points to work on constitutional carry and the Second Amendment Preservation Act, and to the tax bill he says he passed with House Republicans.

Retired Navy commander running for Congress. Bob Smith's campaign says he enlisted in the Navy and rose to commander over 26 years, including combat deployments, and was named the Navy's engineer of the year in 2023. It says he holds engineering degrees and lives in Carpinteria with his family. He says he would cut wasteful spending, lower housing, energy, and food costs, and expand homeownership while protecting Social Security and Medicare. He says schools should emphasize reading, math, and STEM, plus vocational paths and research ties to local universities. He says immigration policy should secure the border, remove people convicted of violent crimes, and update farmworker visas.

Candidate for governor of Maine. Bobby Charles says he grew up in Wayne, Maine, the son of a public-school teacher, and later studied at Dartmouth, Oxford, and Columbia Law. He says he is running for safer streets, lower taxes, stronger schools, and a government that works for residents. He says he would cut crime and treat the drug trade as a central threat to Maine communities. He says he would cut taxes and regulation that he argues weigh on businesses and working families. He says schools should improve and that too much state policy has been driven by ideological agendas he opposes.

Musician and small-business owner running for Congress. Bobby Pulido's campaign says he was born and raised in Edinburg, studied political science, and became a well-known Tejano singer while also running businesses. It says he and his wife are raising four sons in the Rio Grande Valley. He says he would challenge corporations raising prices, cut red tape for small businesses, and back apprenticeships and higher-wage jobs that stay in South Texas. He says farmers and ranchers need fair markets and open trade, and that tariffs are raising costs. He says the border should stay secure and violent criminals should be removed, without raids that he argues hurt local workers and businesses.

U.S. representative and ranking Democrat on Education and the Workforce. His campaign says he grew up in Newport News and has represented Virginia's 3rd District since 1993. It says he is known as one of the hardest-working members of Congress and is fighting for students, workers, families, and seniors. He says he authored legislation to raise the federal minimum wage gradually to $17 an hour and the PRO Act on the right to organize. He says he was a lead author of the Every Student Succeeds Act and is fighting to make college more affordable through his College Affordability Act. He says he was the House sponsor of the Post-9/11 G.I. Bill and is leading work on evidence-based criminal-justice reform.

U.S. representative for Minnesota's 1st District. Brad Finstad's office says he is a fourth-generation farmer from the New Ulm area who won a special election in 2022. He and his wife Jackie, who met on the school bus in second grade, have seven children and run an agriculture business alongside their family farm. He earned a University of Minnesota degree in agricultural education. His office says his work as Minnesota's USDA Rural Development director supported rural infrastructure, business development, homeownership, schools, public safety, health care, and high-speed internet. He previously served three terms in the Minnesota Legislature and held executive roles with the Minnesota Turkey Growers Association and the Center for Rural Policy and Development.
District 13 · U.S. House · North Carolina · Republican

Former federal prosecutor and U.S. representative for North Carolina's 13th District. His campaign says he and his wife grew up in Raleigh and are raising two daughters there, and that he resigned as a federal prosecutor in eastern North Carolina to run in 2024. He says he is running again so the district stays safer and more prosperous. He says he would finish the border wall and send an immigrant who commits a felony to prison for at least five years before deportation. He says he supports school choice, a balanced-budget amendment, and police, and he opposes new gun laws aimed at law-abiding owners. He says he is pro-life, supports state laws protecting the unborn, and would defend faith-based pregnancy centers.
District 10 · U.S. House · New York · Democratic

Former New York City comptroller running for Congress in New York's 10th District. His campaign says he organized tenants and built affordable housing at the Fifth Avenue Committee and the Pratt Center, then passed wage laws for gig workers on the City Council and later served as comptroller. It says he was arrested by federal agents while defending immigrants from ICE. He says he would be a check on Donald Trump and fight attacks on immigrants, trans kids, the rule of law, health care, Social Security, and working- and middle-class families. He says Congress should help cities end street homelessness, fix public housing, protect tenants, and build more affordable homes. He says he would take on billionaires and corporate power and get money out of politics rather than take Wall Street, crypto, and AIPAC contributions.

Independent American candidate for secretary of state. Brad Lee Barnhill is the Independent American nominee. His campaign says he has worked about twenty years as a systems analyst and about twenty years as a litigation paralegal. He says that if voters approve voter identification, he would carry it out with the office's existing rules and with help for people who have trouble getting an ID. He says possible duplicate registrations should be reviewed by a person before a record is changed, and that poll rules should be the same in every county. He says he would urge repeal of the commerce tax and oversee the move of business filings from SilverFlume to ORION.

Governor of Idaho, first elected in 2018 and reelected in 2022. His campaign says he is committed to leading so Idahoans can thrive, so children and grandchildren choose to stay, and so people who have left choose to come back. The site calls that experienced leadership the state can trust. His campaign says he cut or simplified 95 percent of Idaho regulations and calls Idaho the least regulated state. His campaign says teacher pay rose, literacy funding increased five-fold, and school-facility spending also worked as property-tax relief, along with new school-choice options and the Idaho LAUNCH program. His campaign says he and the Legislature delivered tax relief with a balanced budget and a AAA credit rating, and that Idaho sent more missions to the border than any other state through an effort he calls Operation No Return.

Former Navy civilian engineer and manufacturer running for Congress. A seventh-generation Hoosier from Brownsburg, he says he spent 25 years in local manufacturing and then nine years as a Navy civilian engineer in electromagnetic warfare after moving to Bloomington. He says he walked away from a secure retirement because he could not ignore the country's direction. He says he supports Medicare for All so no one goes broke trying to stay alive, and he wants higher wages, fair taxes, and restored collective bargaining. He says he is focused on making a first home possible again, lowering the cost of education, and an immigration system that respects the dignity of work. He says policy has shifted wealth upward, and he is running so working people are not left behind from their first jobs through retirement.

U.S. representative running for another term. Brad Sherman's campaign says he was born and raised in Southern California and represents the San Fernando Valley and much of the Westside. It says he is a senior member of Foreign Affairs and Financial Services and helped create the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau. He says he has a perfect rating from the Brady Campaign and an F from the NRA, and he has pushed an assault-weapons ban and longer background checks. He says he cosponsors a safe-storage bill named for a teenager killed by an unsecured firearm. He says he has championed consumer protections and helped create the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau.

Veteran and business owner running for Congress in Wisconsin's 6th District. His campaign says he is a dad, a veteran, and a business builder, and a Democrat running to deliver jobs, affordable health care, and training. He says he wants to protect the Wisconsin he loves. He supports a higher minimum wage, apprenticeships, prevailing wage, project labor agreements, and the right to organize, plus training through tech schools, college, and trades. He says health care should protect people with pre-existing conditions and stay close to home, and he wants transparency before large data centers are built. As a gun owner, he supports background checks, red-flag laws, and secure storage, and he also calls for fair milk prices, farm broadband, reproductive freedom, and LGBTQ+ protections.

U.S. representative running for another term. Brandon Gill's campaign says he was born on an Air Force base, grew up on a cattle ranch outside Abilene, and graduated from Dartmouth before working in finance and starting a conservative news site. It says his father was a fighter pilot and his grandfather a Dallas-area preacher. He says that in Congress he has worked to stop a large tax increase, secure the southern border, and end funding for projects he calls leftist. He says he is running again so children can live in a better Texas and a better America, alongside an America First agenda.

Firearms entrepreneur running for Congress. Brandon Herrera's campaign says he is an entrepreneur and Second Amendment activist with family roots in Texas, including Hispanic heritage and parents from military families. It says he studied pre-law and then built a small firearm-manufacturing business. He says he would take practical steps to secure the southern border and improve support for veterans and their families. He says he would seek national concealed-carry reciprocity, pledge no new taxes, cut waste, and back the REINS Act.

Union leader and Democrat running for Congress. His campaign says he was raised in Copan, returned to Bartlesville as a third-generation union worker, and spent 26 years in leadership with IUOE Local 351. He says he is the son of a Vietnam Army veteran and serves as secretary of the Oklahoma Democratic Party Veterans Federation. He says health care should be affordable for everyone and not tied to a job, and that he would protect women's health care choices and strengthen Social Security and Medicare. He says the economy should grow from the working class up, with fair wages, safe workplaces, and corporations and the wealthy paying their fair share. He says he would fully fund public schools, modernize immigration, and defend the rights of women, LGBTQ+ people, immigrants, and minorities.

Business owner and victims' rights advocate running for Oakland mayor. Brenda Grisham says she is a longtime community advocate and business owner who has stood with Oakland families for safer neighborhoods. She says she announced for mayor in 2025 and is on the November 3, 2026 ballot. She says she will focus on safer neighborhoods and stronger public safety. She says city government should be more accountable and transparent, and that local businesses need support to grow. She says she wants more stable housing, cleaner streets, and stronger neighborhood services.

U.S. representative for Pennsylvania's 2nd District. His campaign says he grew up in a Philadelphia rowhouse, was the first in his family to attend college, and later earned a public-policy degree from Harvard. It says his father was a SEPTA custodian who emigrated from Ireland and that Boyle was elected to the House in 2014. He says his work on the Budget Committee is aimed at a federal budget that expands opportunity. On Ways and Means, he says he wants tax and social policy that matches the priorities of working families. He says the Blue Collar Caucus he co-founded in 2016 looks at wage stagnation, job insecurity, trade, offshoring, and careers in manufacturing and the building trades.

Iowa attorney general and former Guthrie County attorney. The campaign says Iowans elected her attorney general and that she is the first Republican to hold the office since 1979. She was Guthrie County attorney from 2018, a prosecutor since 2016, and president of the Iowa County Attorneys Association, and she previously was counsel to Governor Terry Branstad. She says she has worked to get criminals off the street, advocate for crime victims, and stand with law enforcement. She says that as counsel to Governor Branstad she fought federal health-care policy and rules from other states that she says tried to dictate Iowa farm practices. She says she led a fight against EPA regulations that were hurting Iowa farmers and will use the office to defend what she calls the rule of law.

Insurance agency owner and Republican nominee for Florida's 20th District His campaign says he is a Pompano Beach small-business owner who spent 16 years in insurance and founded Pilgrim Bay Insurance Agency in 2010. He is the son of a public-school teacher and a union worker, holds a finance degree from Nichols College, and is raising a daughter in Pompano Beach with his wife, Yula, who was born in Venezuela. He says housing and insurance costs are pricing Broward families out, and that 16 years in insurance is what he would take to Congress. He says he would fight the higher grocery, energy, and health-care bills hitting working families. He says he supports legal immigration and a functioning asylum system, and opposes what he calls open borders.
No 2026 issue list was found for this candidate.

State senator and funeral-business owner running for Congress in Tennessee's 9th District. His campaign says he is a small-business owner in the funeral business and a West Tennessee state senator. He says he is ready to take that work to Congress. No 2026 issue list was found for this candidate.

Hawaii Senate minority leader The campaign says Brenton Awa is Hawaii's Senate minority leader, representing Kaneohe through the North Shore, and that he was first elected in 2022. He says he is running for the U.S. House so the 2nd District has more leverage in Washington. He wants to limit corporate purchases of single-family homes and open suitable federal land for local workforce housing. U.S. representative for Pennsylvania's 17th District. His campaign says he is a Thornburg native, Naval Academy graduate, and Iraq war veteran who later worked as a voting-rights lawyer at the Brennan Center and at the University of Pittsburgh. It says he has represented western Pennsylvania since 2022 and lives in Allegheny County with his wife and four children. He says he is fighting powerful interests he argues have taken the American Dream away from working people. Before Congress he says he worked on voting rights and election security, and he helped University of Pittsburgh faculty win a union with the United Steelworkers.

Lawyer and business owner running for Congress. Chris Gober's campaign says he is a seventh-generation Texan, a Texas A&M graduate, and a Harvard-trained lawyer who grew up in Throckmorton and Graham. It says he worked on national security and border issues at the Justice Department, then built businesses in Texas, and is a husband and father of two. He says he would make life affordable, secure the border against cartels, and stop what he calls the weaponization of government against conservatives. He says he would grow defense and technology jobs in Austin and the Brazos Valley so the country outcompetes China. He says rural communities need fewer regulations, nearby health care, and data-center rules that do not drain water or raise electric rates.

Attorney and small-business owner running for Georgia's 11th District. His campaign says he grew up in a trailer park in Rossville, worked full time while going to school at night, and drove a forklift and loaded trucks before becoming an attorney. He says he is a husband and father of triplets, and that for more than fourteen years he has worked as a parent-defense attorney. He says he would make health care more affordable, expand Affordable Care Act premium tax credits, lower prescription costs, and improve access in rural communities. He says he takes no corporate PAC money, would ban members of Congress and their immediate families from trading individual stocks, and would cut taxes for working and middle-class families. He says data centers should not shift water and power costs onto ordinary customers, and he would invest in affordable energy and modernize the grid, roads, and bridges.

U.S. Senate candidate of the Oregon Progressive Party and the Pacific Green Party. His site lists his work as a long-haul truck driver and a UAW aircraft mechanic, and civic roles that include the Oregon Consumer League, a neighborhood association, and union shop steward. He says no special interest is funding the campaign. He says he would cut the military budget, support Medicare for All, and raise wages while rejecting both broad tariffs and trade deals that override labor and environmental rules. He proposes a federal fund for earthquake retrofits, backup power, and supplies ahead of a Cascadia earthquake. His site says state law can end a smaller party that misses a statewide vote threshold, and that this Senate race is the Progressive Party's contest this year.

Candidate for Congress The campaign says Chris Jones grew up in Pine Bluff as the son of a minister and built a career in science without leaving Arkansas behind. He says he is running to expand opportunity, strengthen schools and health care, and give more Arkansans a seat at the table. He says the economy should mean good jobs, fair wages, small-business growth, reliable internet, and rural hospitals that stay open. He wants stronger schools, maternal health care, addiction recovery, and food security for families. He supports early childhood education, apprenticeships, and training in both technology and the trades, plus fair maps and elections people can trust.

Former police officer and prosecutor running for attorney general. Chris Mann's site says he followed his father into law enforcement, left uniformed work after a drunk driver hit him during a traffic stop, and then prosecuted cases as an assistant district attorney in Wyandotte County and as a senior staff attorney at the Kansas Securities Commission. He says the attorney general should answer when local departments ask for help investigating and prosecuting major crimes, including drug distribution and child sexual abuse. He wants officer training held around the state, mental-health care for first responders, and workers' compensation coverage for PTSD. He says he will prosecute scams, push treatment access outside the northeast corner of the state, and fund shelters for people leaving domestic violence.

Fourth-generation Iowan and military veteran running for Congress. He says he was born and raised in Iowa's 4th District, that his children are the fifth generation in northwest Iowa, and that his family has farm ties around Fonda. He says he took an oath when he entered the military, is the son of a Vietnam veteran, and studied law. He says he will work with the Trump administration to secure the border, stop fentanyl, and support immigration enforcement. He says standing up for agriculture means protecting markets, defending landowner rights, and backing trade agreements for what farmers produce. He says he will put America first, stand up to China, bring jobs back, restore energy independence, and defend life from conception to natural death.

U.S. representative running for the Senate. Chris Pappas's campaign says he is in the House and will take on corporate interests, Donald Trump, or his own party when he thinks New Hampshire is better served. He says he forced a House vote on banning stock trading by members of Congress, including against his own party's leadership. He says he took on drug companies to lower prices and cap insulin at $35. He says he is challenging polluters of drinking water and companies he describes as taking advantage of veterans.

State representative running for Congress in Pennsylvania's 3rd District. Chris Rabb is a five-term Pennsylvania state representative from Philadelphia. His campaign says he is running to put working people ahead of corporate power. His platform calls for housing people can afford, a living wage, and Medicare for All. He also says he will fight for food security, clean air and water, and a foreign policy that prioritizes peace.

Disabled Army veteran and IBEW Local 1 member running for Missouri's 8th District. He says he is a second-generation union electrician from Arnold running a grassroots campaign that takes no corporate PAC or dark money. He supports the PRO Act to protect organizing and the Major Richard Star Act so combat-injured veterans receive full benefits. He wants the United States kept out of another long war and supports a bill to count the full human and financial cost of war up front. He wants Citizens United overturned and backs the Equality Act, and he says rural hospitals and public schools in the district are underfunded.

Retired Navy SEAL and Republican nominee for Congress The campaign says Chris Shea is a Watertown native, retired Navy SEAL, firefighter, former small-business owner, and the Republican nominee in Connecticut's 5th District. He served with SEAL teams and at the Pentagon over a career of more than 30 years, and he and his wife, Anita, raised their daughter in Watertown. His campaign slogan is lowering costs, growing wages, and protecting America. He says that experience, from a small business that employed six people to helping veterans start new careers, is what he would bring to Congress.

Candidate for Congress campaigning on north Missouri farms, taxes, and rural hospitals. His issues page presents a conservative platform he ties to President Trump, aimed at gun rights, small-town hospitals, abortion, taxes, and agriculture. He says the Second Amendment is not negotiable and that he will oppose federal gun restrictions aimed at law-abiding owners. He wants less red tape for rural hospitals, and he opposes taxpayer funding of abortion. He supports making the Trump tax cuts permanent and giving farms more market access with fewer regulations.

U.S. representative for Pennsylvania's 6th District. Chrissy Houlahan is a third-generation veteran, an Air Force Reserve captain, and a former AND1 executive and Teach for America corps member who was the first woman elected in Pennsylvania's 6th District. She serves on Armed Services and Intelligence and chairs the BIOTech Caucus. She says her work in Congress is aimed at the cost of living for families in Chester County and the district. Through the BIOTech Caucus she says she is working to grow jobs tied to biotechnology.

Former county attorney running for Congress. Christian Menefee's campaign says he was raised in the 18th District by two military parents, used a Pell Grant to become the first in his family to finish college, and earned a law degree at Washington University. It says he was a commercial litigator and then the youngest person, and the first Black person, elected Harris County attorney. He says he would seek Medicare for All, protect public schools and abortion rights, and make daily life more affordable. He lists workers' rights, jobs, gun-violence prevention, immigration, veterans, and criminal-justice reform among his priorities. He says he went to court against voting restrictions, pollution in Black and Latino neighborhoods, and disaster price gouging.

Teacher and union organizer running for Congress in Michigan's 5th District. His campaign says he was born and raised in Michigan, the son of an immigrant family on his father's side and of Michigan ministers on his mother's, and that he worked his way through school as a bricklayer. He says he is a husband, father, and teacher. He says he would fight for living wages, union jobs, and an economy that rewards hard work. He says quality, affordable health care is a right, and he wants housing working families can afford. He also calls for education and job training, and says he would put people ahead of corporate and billionaire interests.

Law professor, engineer, and former state representative running for Congress. She says she is a mom running so Iowa's working families come ahead of the wealthy and well-connected. After 26 years teaching constitutional law at the University of Iowa, she says she feels a duty to defend self-government against money and partisanship. She says her top priority is lowering the cost of living: end tariffs she says raise family costs, stop hedge funds from buying family homes, build more housing, let Medicare negotiate more drug prices, and cap insulin at $35 a month. She says she takes no corporate PAC money and would ban stock trading by members of Congress and other high officials, seek a constitutional amendment to overturn Citizens United, and set term limits. She says her father's insurer canceled coverage after he became ill, and she wants a health system that does not drop people when they get sick.

Prosecutor running for Congress in Michigan's 10th District. Her campaign says she grew up in Macomb County, attended the University of Michigan and Wayne State University Law School, and worked as a prosecutor on homicide, trafficking, and sexual-assault cases. She and her husband David are raising three children in Macomb County. She says she would lower the cost of groceries, gas, and health care and fight for good-paying Michigan jobs. She says she would support safer communities, schools, and law-enforcement resources to prevent violent crime and protect children and seniors online. She says she refuses corporate PAC money, would ban members of Congress from trading stocks, and would work with either party against corruption.

Candidate for governor of Oregon. Her campaign says Oregon should be the best place to raise a family, start a business, buy a home, and get a strong education, and that those goals are out of reach for too many people. She says the cost of living, jobs leaving the state, homelessness, schools, and state spending are leadership problems. She says she would order agencies to find rules and fees that raise the cost of housing, energy, food, child care, health care, and running a business, and that she would veto new tax and fee increases. She says she would speed housing permits, expand help for first-time buyers, and make it easier to build more kinds of homes. She says homelessness spending should be audited and shifted toward addiction recovery, mental-health treatment, and programs measured by how many people reach stable housing.

Candidate for Michigan secretary of state. She says the office should administer elections and serve residents, and that it should not be a partisan platform or a step toward higher office. She says more than a decade in health care shaped her view that individual rights and dignity are not negotiable. She says she would keep voter rolls accurate, let people verify how elections are run, and treat independent and minor-party candidates fairly. She wants government limited to protecting rights, maintaining essential services, and enforcing laws consistently. She says she would restrict mass surveillance, including vehicle-tracking cameras and unchecked data collection, and push open records and plain-language budget reports.

Retired Approval Voting Party candidate for the U.S. Senate. He told the Fort Collins Coloradoan he is retired and is running to publicize approval voting. He does not have a campaign website. He says people should be able to support a lesser-known candidate without taking a vote away from a major-party candidate. He says government should be smaller. He says the national debt should be eliminated.

Kentucky Party candidate for U.S. Senate. Christopher Campbell's site says he is a dues-paying member of a labor union, served in the Kentucky National Guard, and is a Kentucky Colonel. He supports Medicare for All and says the federal government should provide basic medical care. He says workers need safe conditions, strong benefits, good pay, and a way to raise grievances without retaliation. He wants a constitutional environmental amendment and a ban on carbon credits that he says let facilities keep polluting.
District 1 · U.S. House · New York · Democratic

Military pilot and union leader running for Congress in New York's 1st District. His campaign says he joined the New York Army National Guard at 17, deployed to Kuwait, and later worked as an FAA air traffic controller, a union leader, and a volunteer firefighter. He says he is running to bring that same discipline to Congress for the Long Island district where he grew up. He says he would seek federal investments that reduce the cost of housing, energy, and basic goods for Long Island families. He says he would protect Medicare and Medicaid and push changes that expand access and lower out-of-pocket costs for older adults. He also says he would press for long-term investment in the shoreline and for the tools first responders need to keep neighborhoods safe.

Coast Guard veteran and federal law enforcement officer running for Congress The campaign says Christopher Lancia was born and raised in Bridgeport, served in the Coast Guard, and later worked as a federal law enforcement officer. He now lives in Milford and says he is running to give Connecticut a voice in an America First agenda. He says border security is national security and that he wants the border chaos stopped. He says he will fight for lower taxes, a balanced budget, and an end to spending he ties to inflation. He supports term limits, the Second Amendment, and law enforcement, and says parents should control decisions about their children's education.
District 4 · U.S. House · New Jersey · Republican

U.S. representative for New Jersey's 4th District. His campaign says he has served 46 years and is running again after Ocean and Monmouth County Republican conventions endorsed him. It says he is known for constituent work and for turning local problems into national law. He says his laws cover veterans' health care and benefits, autism, Lyme disease, Alzheimer's, and international parental child abduction. He says he wrote the Trafficking Victims Protection Act and later anti-trafficking laws, and that he is worried crowded events such as the World Cup raise trafficking risks. He says he backed the Working Families Tax Cut and has fought offshore wind projects he says endanger the Jersey coast.

Republican candidate for U.S. House in Colorado's 1st District. Christy Peterson's campaign says she is the Republican candidate for Congress in the 1st District, covering Denver and parts of northern Arapahoe County. She says she is running on common sense, safe cities, a strong economy, and safe schools. She says she stands for low taxes, limited government, and peace through strength. She says she would review Social Security's finances so the program can stay solvent, and that she would cut the federal debt. She says she supports Colorado's Taxpayer's Bill of Rights.

America First Party candidate for U.S. Senate in Nebraska. His campaign says he has lived in Nebraska his whole life, the oldest of seven in an Irish Catholic home, and that he has worked since he was 12, including in management, sales, and as a vice president of a meatpackers and butchers union. He says his views line up with the America First Party. He says he would secure the southern border, expand immigration enforcement, deport people he says have no claim to remain, and put citizens, veterans, and workers first for taxpayer resources. He says Social Security must be protected with no benefit cuts before a 2032 insolvency date, and he opposes endless foreign wars and blank checks to other governments. He also calls for affordable college, an end to crushing student debt, a return of trade schools, lower health-care costs, and help with child care for working parents.

U.S. representative for Tennessee's 3rd District. His campaign describes him as a fiscal and social conservative representing Tennessee's 3rd District. He says massive federal spending meant to stem unemployment is counterproductive, and that the tax system does not support the growth the economy needs. He says the country's founding values still matter to him, and that environmentally safe energy exploration should be part of energy policy.

Wyoming secretary of state and candidate for Congress The campaign says Chuck Gray served six years in the Wyoming House before becoming secretary of state, an office that also serves as lieutenant governor. It says he has focused on election administration, energy, and abortion limits. His campaign says he will protect coal, oil, and gas jobs, oppose what he calls woke wind projects and ESG rules, and fight inflation with lower taxes and less spending. The site says he sponsored Wyoming's voter ID law, required proof of citizenship to register, and banned ranked-choice voting and foreign funding of elections. It says he supports securing the border, the Second Amendment, and pro-life policies, and opposes taxpayer-funded abortion.
District 5 · U.S. House · North Carolina · Democratic

Journalist running for Congress in North Carolina's 5th District. His campaign says he is a Wilkes County native who started at his grandfather's paper, the Wilkes Journal-Patriot, and spent more than 40 years as a local journalist after graduating from Wofford College. He and his wife Shari live in Wilkesboro. He says he would raise the minimum wage, shift taxes toward the wealthy, and support public schools, small businesses, and farms. He says he would protect Medicare, Medicaid, Social Security, and veterans' benefits, and add a public option so rural towns have a hospital nearby. He says abortion belongs between a patient and a doctor, and he wants to overturn Citizens United and ban members of Congress from trading stocks.

Former mayor and retired law-enforcement officer running for Congress. Chuong Vo's campaign says he is a husband, a father, a former mayor of Cerritos, and a 28-year law-enforcement officer who answered 911 calls for nearly three decades. It says his wife is a classroom teacher and that his family, like many immigrant families, was given a chance in this country. He says he is running to keep families safe, lower costs, and hold government accountable. He says that on the council he focused on safe neighborhoods, responsive city services, and balanced budgets. He says he returned campaign contributions after a council election and supports ending insider stock trading in Congress.

Democratic candidate for governor and a former executive councilor. Cinde Warmington is the Democratic nominee for governor. Her campaign says she was the only Democrat on the Executive Council and is running on the cost of living. She says she would repeal the private-school voucher program, which she argues drives up property taxes and hurts public schools. She says she would push back on higher health-care costs and tariffs, and would reject an immigration detention site in Merrimack. She says she would not support a sales or income tax, and that she would work for small businesses.

Kansas state senator running for governor. Cindy Holscher's site says she was raised on a farm and that her work in the Legislature included cleaning up after a failed tax experiment, lowering costs, and making health care more accessible. She says she will lower the cost of living, including health care, housing, child care, and groceries, and fully fund public schools. She says she will expand Medicaid, protect rural hospitals, and protect Social Security, Medicare, and Medicaid. She calls for a pause on new data centers until guardrails are set, and she supports legalizing recreational and medical marijuana.

U.S. senator from Mississippi seeking another term. She says rumors that she would not run again are false and that she is definitely planning to campaign for reelection. She says the campaign is a grassroots fight for conservative leadership for Mississippi. Her campaign issues page highlights Second Amendment rights and balancing the budget. It also highlights health care and defending unborn life. It lists stopping illegal immigration and supporting the military and veterans.

Attorney running for Congress. Claire Reynolds's campaign says she grew up in central Illinois, studied journalism at Northwestern, and earned a law degree at the University of San Diego. It says she moved to Texas in 2007, raised her children here, and is the Democratic candidate in a district that now stretches from north Austin to Midland and Odessa. She says wages have not kept up with prices and that nobody should go bankrupt over a broken hip or cancer. She supports moving toward single-payer coverage like Medicare, a strong border with a faster legal immigration process, and abortion that is safe, legal, and rare. She says Texas needs both oil and gas and renewable energy jobs to stay competitive.
District 7 · U.S. House · New York · Democratic

State assemblymember running for Congress in New York's 7th District. Her campaign says she is a union organizer, artist, and democratic socialist, and a dual citizen of the Ysleta del Sur Pueblo Nation and the United States. It says she worked low-wage jobs, helped democratize UAW Local 2110 at Columbia, and has used her Assembly seat to tax the rich and protect tenants. She says she would strengthen the PRO Act, give active federal support to union organizing, and end at-will employment. She says everyone should be able to count on a living-wage job, paid parental and sick leave, health care, and a dignified retirement. She says the campaign will not take corporate PAC or dark money.
District 24 · U.S. House · New York · Republican

U.S. representative for New York's 24th District. Her campaign says she is an attorney and businesswoman whose view of public service was shaped by running a small business while raising her son as a single mother. It says she served six years in the state Assembly before her election to Congress. She says she has led efforts against Chinese theft of American intellectual property and against China's grip on the financial system. She says the border has to be secured now, that Social Security and Medicare are personal because her parents relied on them, and that the Second Amendment is a way of life in Upstate New York. She also says the health-care system is not working and that Congress has to deliver solutions, and she highlights veterans' issues as what she calls a Marine mom.

U.S. representative for Georgia's 14th District. His office says he was district attorney for the Lookout Mountain Judicial Circuit and is a lieutenant colonel in the Air National Guard. He says he was a White House Fellow in 2018 and 2019, serving in the vice president's office and the Defense Department. Raised in the North Georgia mountains, he captained the basketball team at Emory, then earned a master's from Cornell and a law degree from Southern Methodist University. He says he is fighting for President Trump's agenda to bring manufacturing jobs back to northwest Georgia. He says he supports removing people who are in the country without permission, and that border security is national security. He says he would defend the First and Second Amendments, and keep working to stop fentanyl trafficking in northwest Georgia.

Candidate for Congress in Louisiana's 3rd District. His campaign site says he is a lifelong Louisiana resident who served in Acadiana law enforcement and trained as a military police officer in the Army. It calls him a defender of the Bill of Rights. He says a sworn officer's oath is to the Constitution, not to a sheriff, chief, or marshal. The site says that, as a Christian, he focuses on the power of an individual to be redeemed.

Community volunteer running for Congress in Ohio's 3rd District. Cleophus Dulaney says he lives and works in the district and has spent years helping people who are homeless, encouraging young people, and backing candidates in both parties. He says he is running because politics has too much party loyalty and not enough listening. He says he will push Medicare to negotiate drug prices, take on pharmacy middlemen, and support tax relief for working and middle-class families. He also wants infrastructure, manufacturing, and clean-energy jobs, apprenticeships, and fewer rules that do not make small businesses safer, plus voting-rights protections and fair maps.

U.S. representative for Oregon's 2nd District, seeking another term. His campaign says he is a third-generation Oregonian raised on cattle ranches in Harney County, a lawyer who has practiced in Ontario since 1977, and a former chair of the Oregon Water Resources Commission. It says he served in the Oregon House and Senate before running for Congress. He says he will back tighter border security and finishing a border wall, and he describes himself as a right-to-life candidate who believes life begins at conception. He opposes government-run health care and says he will direct investment toward rural Oregon while holding the federal government accountable for how it manages forests and wildfire. He says he supports the Second Amendment and the wise use of Oregon's water and land.

Democratic nominee for Mississippi's 1st District. His campaign says he is a fifth-generation Mississippian living in rural Lafayette County with his wife of 35 years, and that his career has been spent speaking up for people who are vulnerable. A campaign release calls him a civil rights attorney. He says he wants to combat inflation and the policies driving up costs for Mississippians. He says he will protect and expand affordable health care. He says north Mississippi should get its fair share of federal dollars for economic development, infrastructure, and struggling schools, and he wants the right to have a vote counted preserved.

Retired Army first sergeant running for Congress The campaign says Clyde Jones served 21 years in the Army Signal Corps, retired as a first sergeant, and received a Bronze Star for service in Desert Storm and Iraqi Freedom. He later worked in process safety for DuPont and FMC in south Alabama and serves as an associate minister. He says he will focus on lowering prices for gas, health coverage, rent, and groceries. He says Congress should check the White House, and he says he will not take corporate PAC money. He supports expanding Medicaid and Affordable Care Act premium tax credits so people who earn too much for Medicaid can still get coverage.

Republican candidate for Nevada's 4th District. His campaign says he is a fourth-generation Nevadan, a small-business owner, and a rancher who has also coached young athletes. He says he is running because Washington is not working for Nevada. He says he wants housing, health care, groceries, and energy to be more affordable. He says tipped workers should not be taxed on tips and that overtime pay should be defended. He says waste, fraud, and abuse should be eliminated so Medicaid and Social Security last, and he wants more quality schools and career pathways.
District 8 · U.S. House · North Carolina · Democratic

Small-business owner running for Congress in North Carolina's 8th District. His campaign says he was born and raised in Union County, started in masonry, was homeschooled, and worked in construction and farming before starting a business more than a decade ago. He says he and his wife have two children and that he never planned to run. He says he will not take money from lobbyists for corporate or foreign interests and will not trade stocks in office. He says homeownership should be back in reach and that health care should heal people rather than maximize profit. He says markets should reward work and entrepreneurship, and that corporate monopolies are squeezing small businesses and family farms.

Former U.S. representative running for Congress. Colin Allred's campaign says he was raised in Dallas by a single mother who taught in public school, captained the Baylor football team, played in the NFL, and became a civil rights lawyer. It says he worked at the Department of Housing and Urban Development and later won a House seat. He says he is running to lower costs and stop politicians from rigging the economy against people who work hard. He says his earlier service included work on voting rights and on VA care in North Texas.
Governor and lieutenant governor · Illinois · Independent

With Carolyn Schofield, a former McHenry County Board member · Palatine consultant Owner of Cor Strategies. A Republican strategist for about 20 years who left the party to run. This guide has no separate photo of Schofield. He calls affordability the race and says neither major-party nominee will fix property taxes. Property-tax relief first, then spending restraint, cheaper gas and power, fewer data centers, and more housing. Has proposed taxing some services so property taxes and the sales tax on essentials can come down. Supports abortion rights. Would amend the TRUST Act so police can work with federal agents on violent cases. Supports more gun laws and health-care price transparency, including direct primary care.

Contract manager and farmer Colt Shelby says he worked on drilling rigs for nearly 16 years and has spent the last twenty years managing hundreds of millions of dollars in contracts. He says he got into the race in 2024 after a 3,000-bed prison was proposed near his home. He says he will open government records and restore what he calls honest government. He opposes school voucher plans that he says pull money away from rural public schools. He opposes the proposed Franklin County prison, and he says data-center expansion should not raise utility rates for families and farms.

Congress votes, added across the communities

San Francisco supervisor running for Congress. Connie Chan's campaign says she was born in Hong Kong, moved to San Francisco at 13, and graduated from Galileo High School and UC Davis. It says she is the District 1 supervisor and has chaired the Board of Supervisors budget committee since 2023. She says Washington should stop cutting public programs to pay for tax breaks for billionaires and corporations, and should rebuild worker bargaining power. She says she would reform the tax and budget system and defend rights she says are under threat. She points to her work on affordable housing, small-business and union protections, and legal help for immigrants facing enforcement.

First-generation farmer from north Louisiana running for Congress. He says he knows hard work and keeping his word, and that he cannot be bought by lobbyists or billionaires. He is running so someone in Washington fights for people he calls hard-working patriots who are tired of being left behind. He says he would raise wages, protect the right to organize, and shift power from corporations to the people who do the work. He says more than a third of the district relies on Medicaid, that he supports Medicare for All, and that health care should depend on need rather than income. He says he would open public grocery stores stocked with local food that SNAP and WIC can buy, and he supports overturning Citizens United and banning congressional stock trading.
Valid votes, added across the provinces and territories · Canada
Valid votes, added across the provinces and territories

Candidate for U.S. Senate. Cory Booker's campaign calls him a fighter for New Jersey and says the effort is aimed at justice and opportunity. The site says the campaign takes no money from federal lobbyists, corporate PACs, or executives in the fossil-fuel and pharmaceutical industries. It asks supporters to give directly and says the campaign is powered by grassroots donors.
District 4 · U.S. House · South Carolina · Democratic

Civil-rights advocate running for Congress. Her campaign says she was born and raised in Spartanburg, in a family that has lived there for more than two centuries, and that she holds degrees in journalism and communications and a master's in political science from Howard University. She says she has worked as a legislative page, a Clyburn Fellow, and a lobbyist on reproductive health, public education, elections, guns, and criminal justice. She says her Upstate First agenda would expand health care, build affordable homes, manage rapid growth, invest in small businesses, and stop data centers from coming into local communities. She says she would fight for stronger schools, fair wages, safer communities, the power of every vote, and veterans. She says she is committed to a more affordable and inclusive future for Greenville and Spartanburg.

U.S. representative running for another term. Craig Goldman's campaign says he is a fifth-generation Texan and fourth-generation Fort Worth native who spent 12 years in the Texas House, including as chair of Energy Resources, before his election to Congress. It says he serves on Energy and Commerce, which covers energy, health, and telecommunications. He says his first bill signed into law rolled back regulations he argues would have cost Americans billions, and that he voted to extend the 2017 tax cuts. He says he supported the Laken Riley Act so immigration authorities detain people in the country illegally who are accused of theft or assault. He says border security is the federal government's first duty and that he backed more defense spending to keep building the F-35.

Manufacturing executive running for Congress. Cristian Morales's campaign says he was born in Guatemala, came to the United States with his family in the 1970s, and earned degrees from Purdue and Cornell. It says he has spent more than 20 years in automotive, aerospace, and defense manufacturing. He says he wants better education and job skills, a state where business is affordable, and more work for blue-collar families. He says immigration, housing costs, crime, homelessness, health care, and civil rights are the pillars of his campaign. He says government should protect freedoms, secure the border, and stay accountable rather than grow larger.
Second votes in the whole country · Germany
Second votes in the whole country

Former city commissioner and Democratic nominee for Florida's 18th District His campaign says he is a former Lake Wales city commissioner, the manager of Eagle Ridge Mall, a restaurant owner, and a husband and father of five. He says that under his management the mall grew from 35 to 71 stores, and that he and his wife are raising their children in Lake Wales. He says he would push a federal reinsurance backstop to bring down property-insurance premiums. He says veterans should get timely local care, including covered local providers when the VA cannot see them nearby soon enough. He says he would keep property taxes from pushing out homeowners, seniors, and working families, and support citrus growers against disease and unchecked development.
No 2026 issue list was found for this candidate.

Candidate for governor of Oklahoma. Her campaign says a campaign should be about people, and she is asking Oklahomans to send stories, photos, and letters about why they love the state. She says those stories would guide her if she becomes governor. No 2026 issue list was found for this candidate.

Teacher and small-business owner running for Indiana's 6th District. She says she is a seventh-generation Hoosier who, with her husband Trent, raised two children in Columbus and has owned a community business for more than 20 years. She taught biology and environmental science for more than a decade at Columbus Signature Academy and later served as a science and education fellow in the U.S. House. She earned a biology degree from the University of Evansville, a master's in anthropology from Indiana University, and a doctorate in education policy from Ball State in 2025. She says working-class Hoosiers should have good-paying jobs, affordable housing and child care, and access to sick time and paid family leave. She says she would support professional teachers and neighborhood pre-K through 12 schools that are safe and welcoming for students of all backgrounds and abilities. She says health care should be affordable enough that no one skips treatment because of cost, job loss, or discrimination, and she would invest in cleaner energy and oppose data centers that consume large amounts of fuel, water, and electricity.

Mayor of High Point running for Congress in North Carolina's 6th District. His campaign says he is a husband, father, former teacher, small-business owner, and mayor who was raised in the district. Candidate for Congress The campaign says Dale Strong was born and raised in Monrovia in Madison County and worked as a volunteer firefighter and paramedic before serving as a district commissioner and chairman of the Madison County Commission. Union carpenter running for Congress in New Jersey's 1st District. He says South Jersey families are working harder and falling behind. He says he would cut unnecessary federal spending and regulations, support American energy, and secure the border. He says he would require proof of citizenship and voter identification, and give parents more say over school curriculum. He says he would expand apprenticeships, back law enforcement against fentanyl trafficking, and make health prices and prescriptions more affordable, including through health savings accounts.

Business owner and former state legislator running for governor Dan Ahlers's campaign says he is a business owner, a former Dell Rapids Chamber of Commerce administrator, and a former state legislator who served on the Appropriations Committee. Richardson council member running for Congress. Dan Barrios's campaign says he grew up in a working-class family in Brownsville and has lived in North Texas for more than 25 years. Candidate for governor of Maryland. Dan Cox's campaign describes him as a husband, father, and small-business owner who says he has taken on leaders in both parties. He says he would cut taxes and fees and limit property taxes so retirees are not taxed out of their homes. He proposes down-payment help and tax credits for first-time and younger buyers, and says building and permitting costs should come down. He says Maryland should reopen closed power plants, study small modular reactors, and give households more energy choices so electric bills stop climbing.

Navy reserve officer and Republican nominee for Florida's 9th District His campaign says he was working in the Pentagon on September 11, then joined the Navy and completed four tours in the Middle East and Central Asia, plus a State Department tour in southern Afghanistan. He says he holds the rank of commander, has been selected for promotion to captain, and served with SEAL team deployments in Iraq and Afghanistan. He says he would safeguard constitutional rights and work with President Trump to keep the military funded. He says he would take on overdevelopment and rising property-insurance rates. He says he would lower grocery, gas, and housing costs.

Former White House and Labor Department aide running for Congress. Born and raised in Andover, he says his family came from Korea and Lebanon. He says he is running to defend democracy, protect rights, and reduce the cost of living against what he calls a dismantling of the country. He says that in the Biden administration he worked on infrastructure, clean-energy jobs, education, and lower prescription costs for seniors. He says that at the Labor Department he helped recover wages, improve workplace safety, and increase union participation, and that he takes no corporate PAC money.

U.S. representative for Pennsylvania's 9th District. Dan Meuser describes himself as a job creator who was first elected in 2018 and is serving a fourth term. He sits on Financial Services, where he chairs an oversight subcommittee, and on Small Business. He says his priorities are an America First agenda, border security, the economy, and energy. He says his committee work is aimed at oversight of the financial system and support for small business.

Industrial mechanic, union leader, and Navy veteran. His campaign says he is a Navy veteran, a Nebraska National Guardsman, an industrial mechanic, and a union leader. He says no institution needs fixing more than the Senate, and that he would bring that work history to it. He says people have more in common with each other than with the partisans who run Washington. He says he would protect small businesses, family farms and ranches, and middle-class jobs. He says he would bring Nebraska values to Washington, drawing on his years as a sailor, a guardsman, a mechanic, and a union leader.

Lieutenant governor of Texas, running for re-election. His campaign says he was first elected lieutenant governor in 2014 and re-elected in 2018 and 2022. He says he wants a stronger electric grid through more reliable thermal power and a high-quality education for every student. He says he works to secure the border, support law enforcement, and protect life, religious freedom, and the Second Amendment.

U.S. senator from Alaska Dan Sullivan has served in the U.S. Senate since January 2015 and was reelected in 2020. He was a Marine Corps infantry officer for more than 30 years, retired as a colonel in the Reserve in early 2024, and sits on the Armed Services, Commerce, Environment and Public Works, and Veterans' Affairs committees. He says he is running again to keep developing Alaska's energy resources. His campaign points to a large tax cut and says families and businesses should keep more of what they earn. He cites military investment and a stronger Alaska health-care system as reasons for another term.

Consumer advocate running for Congress in Maryland's 1st District. His campaign says he is a Democrat who has spent more than 14 years working with state banking regulators and the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau to challenge financial fraud. He and his wife Megan live in Bellevue, and he says her work as a nurse practitioner in Dorchester County shapes his view of health-care costs. He says he would hold monthly town halls and support a ban on members of Congress trading stocks, options, and crypto. He says he would fight spending freezes and tariffs that hurt farmers and raise prices, and protect consumers from what he calls corporate grift. He says he would restore safety programs for food, water, bridges, and air travel, protect the environment, and defend affordable care and public-health research.

Small-business owner and third-generation Arizonan running for Congress in Arizona's 7th District. His campaign says he had everything taken from him and battled back to run two businesses. He says he is running to put Arizona families ahead of the Washington establishment. He says he will secure the southern border and fight to give Border Patrol the resources to do the job. He says he will cut taxes and simplify the code for small businesses, and he has proposed a flat tax or a national sales tax that would end the IRS as it exists now. He says he will promote jobs by allowing responsible mining in southern Arizona.

Retired elementary school teacher Daniel J. Nonpartisan candidate for governor and a member of the State Board of Education. Navy veteran and working mother running for Congress in Arizona's 9th District. Her campaign says she lives in Wittmann and served as an operations specialist on the destroyer USS Bainbridge. Health-care worker running for Congress. He says health care is a right and points to Medicare and the VA as models for care that costs less and covers more people. He says he would protect public schools from what he calls billionaire voucher schemes, and he wants Congress to vote before troops are sent into lasting wars. He says immigration policy should combine a secure border with basic dignity, and that small businesses should come ahead of Wall Street.

Public-affairs consultant running for Congress in Tennessee's 7th District. His campaign says he is a husband and father with working-class roots whose father started an industrial uniform company and whose mother worked overnight factory shifts for health benefits. He says student loans and several jobs got him through the University of Richmond, and that he later built the public-affairs firm Calvert Street Group. He says too many politicians are serving billionaires while cutting safety nets, including expanded Medicaid, Medicare, health-care premiums, student loans, and food assistance. He says his career has been about protecting the working and middle class, including work on solar farms, affordable housing, rural hospitals, and transit funding.

Community organizer running for Congress in New York's 13th District. Retired Air Force colonel running for Congress. Former prosecutor and state legislator running for Congress. U.S. representative and former state senator running for another term. He says he cannot be bought and is focused on cleaning up corruption in Washington.

Candidate for governor of Tennessee. He says he was raised in Tennessee, became an engineer, started a small business, and is running to build government that puts people ahead of profit. He calls for a 24-month pause on new data centers, open primaries, fairer districts, and ranked ballots in a future governor's race.

Small-business owner running for Congress in Maryland's 2nd District. He says that work includes opposing socialism and what he describes as strict Sharia law and movements that weaken faith, family, and the Bill of Rights.

Southwest Oregon small businessman running for U.S. Senate. His campaign says he is a third-generation resident who has served in the Oregon Capitol and would carry that work to Washington. He says his approach is to work for constituents rather than political insiders. He says he is running to keep working on solutions for working families, their communities, and the businesses that support them. He says the Senate needs common sense, accountability, and a stronger rural voice so people across Oregon are represented.

Milwaukee County executive and former state representative running for governor. He says he would take a storefront-revitalization program statewide, tie infrastructure spending to local hiring and labor standards, and expand apprenticeships in the trades and health care. He proposes more affordable housing, universal early childhood education, and closing the state's broadband gap. He says he would protect voting rights and push for nonpartisan redistricting.

Republican candidate for Nevada's 2nd District. He says he will fully fund police, seek tougher sentences for violent and repeat offenders, and end what he calls soft-on-crime policies. He says people in the country illegally should be deported, and he supports the SAVE Act, an end to catch-and-release and sanctuary policies, and protection of the Second Amendment.

U.S. Army veteran and retired executive He says he is a former Army sergeant and a retired senior executive, and that he is running from outside a career in politics. Libertarian nominee for U.S. Senate and a solo-practice lawyer. He wants license-plate cameras he says track where people drive taken down unless the government gets a warrant. He also says he will vote to ban congressional stock trading, legalize marijuana, oppose new gun restrictions, defend the unborn, scrap climate mandates, and require Congress to vote before the country goes to war.

Independent candidate for governor of Tennessee. He says he grew up in East Tennessee, built nine companies, kept the jobs in the state, and shared ownership with the people who worked beside him. He says he would pause new data-center approvals until the state writes rules, end tax breaks for them, and send at least half of a data center's new tax revenue to cut property taxes for homeowners in the host county. He says he would create an elected independent state auditor and post disclosable contracts, grants, and payments within 30 days.

Candidate for governor of Florida His campaign says housing costs, underfunded schools, expensive health care, and climate impacts that raise insurance are what Florida families are living with. He says property insurance is the main reason many people cannot afford a place to live. He says a state catastrophic fund that takes natural-disaster risk out of the private market would cut property and car insurance rates, and he supports no-interest state loans for condominium repairs. He says Florida should expand Medicaid and commit to health care for residents across the state. He says the state should pause construction of hyperscale data centers until protections for water and nearby communities are shown to be enough.

U.S. representative for Ohio's 14th District. Dave Joyce says he is a lifelong northeast Ohioan who spent more than 25 years as Geauga County prosecuting attorney and has served in Congress since 2012. His campaign says he is the son of a World War II veteran and is married to a registered nurse. No 2026 issue list was found for this candidate.

U.S. representative and former U.S. attorney for West Tennessee. He says teachers do not need national mandates, that he would secure the border and stop drug trafficking, and that he supports legal immigration for people who follow the rules. He says life begins at conception, that people have a right to keep and bear arms, and that he is working on a farm bill for the district's agriculture.

Candidate for California's 46th Congressional District. Certified teacher running for Congress in Arizona's 3rd District. Independent candidate for the U.S. Senate. He says he is a working Tennessean, not a career politician, and that he is running because party loyalty and special interests have left families behind. U.S. representative for Ohio's 2nd District. David Taylor says he is a Clermont County businessman who runs a ready-mix company, practiced as a local prosecutor, and is married with three daughters. He says health care should be more affordable while protecting seniors, people with low incomes, and people with pre-existing conditions. He says the immigration system is broken and needs a full repair, and he wants Washington to balance its budget.

Independent candidate for governor His campaign says it takes no party, PAC, or corporate money, and that his running mate is Joe Van Vactor. Derek Merrin says he is a former Lucas County state representative who served eight years in the Ohio House and led the House Republican caucus. He also says he played key roles in requiring photo identification to vote and in recognizing a constitutional right to carry a firearm.

U.S. representative for Kansas's 2nd District and a former state attorney general. Derek Schmidt's campaign says he is a fifth-generation Kansan who took office in Congress on January 3, 2025, after serving as attorney general. It says that as attorney general he sued the Biden administration and won, and that he now serves on Armed Services, Judiciary, and Small Business. He says his Armed Services work advocates for Fort Riley, Fort Leavenworth, and Forbes Field, and for service members and their families. On Judiciary, he says he works to secure the southern border, reform the federal bureaucracy, fight taxpayer fraud and abuse, and support law enforcement. On Small Business, he says he works so Kansas small businesses have the resources to grow.

U.S. representative, Army veteran, and small-business owner running for another term. Derek Tran's campaign says he is the son of Vietnamese refugees who worked in the family market, enlisted in the Army at 18, and later opened a law practice for immigrants, workers, and consumers. It says he and his wife, a pharmacist, run an Orange County pharmacy and are raising three children in public schools. He says he has introduced a bill to protect veterans' jobs and reinstate veterans laid off from federal jobs. He says he opposes cuts to Medicaid and Medicare and has fought to lower prescription prices. He says he is defending abortion rights and funding for Planned Parenthood, and he wants higher teacher pay and more vocational training.

U.S. representative and Navy SEAL veteran for Wisconsin's 3rd District. His campaign says he is a Navy SEAL veteran, a paramedic, a father, and a grandfather, and that he is a statesman rather than a politician. He says America is exceptional and Wisconsin is the heart of it. He says life should be protected, drawing on friends lost in training and combat. He says the rights in the Declaration of Independence and the Constitution should not be infringed. He says people do better when government gets out of the way and they can decide what to do with their own money.

Construction business owner running for Congress in New York's 14th District. He says he would focus on affordable rent and quality homes, lower health-care costs by cutting waste and fraud, and lower taxes. He says he would cut red tape and taxes for small businesses so they can grow and hire.

Pharmacist and U.S. representative for Tennessee's 1st District. Her campaign says she was born in Kingsport, grew up in Bloomingdale, and was the first in her family to graduate from college, earning a pharmacy doctorate from Mercer University. She says she has been a licensed pharmacist since 1987 and a business owner for more than 30 years. She says she would finish the border wall, end catch-and-release, restore Remain in Mexico, and defund sanctuary cities. She says she will defend the Second Amendment, support term limits, and treat the opioid crisis with border enforcement, treatment funding, and accountability. Drawing on her pharmacy work, she says health-care choices should stay with patients, drug prices should come down, and the country should not rely on China for medicines.

U.S. representative for Nevada's 1st District The campaign says Dina Titus taught government at the University of Nevada, Las Vegas for 34 years and served 20 years in the Nevada Legislature, including as Democratic minority leader. Democratic candidate for Congress who says faith calls her to speak for people left without help. Her campaign quotes Proverbs 31 and says her faith calls her to speak up for people who are ignored, stand with those who are struggling, and work for a more just and compassionate Texas. She says she is the Democratic candidate for the 25th District. She says real freedom means families can afford to live, communities have a voice, and government answers to the people. She says she will be fair in what she decides and stand up for the rights of people who are suffering and in need.

Rancher, veterinarian, and West Point graduate running for Congress. Don Coover's site says he was born and raised on a small dairy, alfalfa, and soybean farm in southeast Kansas, attended West Point, and now runs a beef-cattle genetics company, a working ranch, and a veterinary practice. He says rising grocery and housing costs and closing local hospitals are leaving people in despair, and that Washington keeps making it worse. He says the district needs people who will work together, spend within their means, and reward hard work. He says he is running so people who know a hard day's work are the ones making decisions again.
District 1 · U.S. House · North Carolina · Democratic

U.S. representative for North Carolina's 1st District. His campaign says he learned the value of hard work in the tobacco fields of eastern North Carolina and is running so the region is not forgotten in Washington. He says families there are dealing with higher gas, grocery, and health-care bills. He says he is working to make life more affordable and to expand opportunity in coastal and rural communities. His campaign lists lowering the cost of living, jobs and economic growth, education, rural infrastructure, and support for the military and veterans.

Libertarian candidate for governor on the Kissick/Mills ticket. The campaign site says the ticket is running because its candidates were tired of choosing between the two major parties. It says it wants a political home for Ohioans who feel they do not have one. The site says too many institutions have become corrupt, self-serving, and comfortable expanding power without representing Ohioans. It says liberty, kindness, justice, common sense, and integrity should be the test for every bill and political leader. It says the campaign will not support a policy that asks voters to give those principles up.

Educator running for Congress in Ohio's 15th District. Don Leonard says he is the son of a single mother and that he saw times when her work was not enough to keep poverty and homelessness away. He says he is running so a full-time job can support a full life for families in central Ohio. He says every American deserves quality insurance they can afford to use, and that every working American should be able to own a home. He also says good child care should not cost as much as a second mortgage, and that seniors should be able to retire with dignity.

Attorney · former Illinois Republican Party chair · won the primary with 40% Springfield lawyer and former chair of the Illinois Gaming Board, from Mt. Sterling. He says he is running on costs, safety, and a voice for the whole state, not only Chicago and Cook County. Lower taxes, energy bills, and health-care costs, with an all-of-the-above energy policy so rates fall and the lights stay on. Back police, hold violent offenders accountable, and enforce immigration law. He opposes taxpayer-funded benefits for people here illegally. Less federal regulation on small business, manufacturing, and farms, and tighter control of federal spending.

U.S. representative and former Virginia lieutenant governor. His official biography says he is in his sixth term representing Arlington, Alexandria, Falls Church, and parts of Fairfax County, and that he serves on Ways and Means and the Joint Economic Committee. He was lieutenant governor from 1990 to 1998 and ambassador to Switzerland and Liechtenstein under President Obama. His biography says his signature work as lieutenant governor included advocacy for Virginians with disabilities and protections for vulnerable people during welfare changes. It says he chaired Jobs for Virginia Graduates, a high-school dropout-prevention program, and served on the D.C. Campaign to Prevent Teen Pregnancy. As ambassador, it says, he pressed for stricter sanctions to push Iran toward nuclear talks and worked against Swiss bank secrecy used by wealthy Americans.
