Former Atlanta mayor running for governor. She was Atlanta's 60th mayor and says she is the first mayor in the city's history to have served in all three branches of city government, as a judge, a city council member, and mayor. She says the city balanced four budgets without a property-tax increase, layoffs, or furloughs, and that reserves stood near $181 million at the end of her term. She says that as mayor she secured major investments in affordable housing and a historic pay raise for Atlanta's first responders. She says she supported small businesses and became a national voice on civil-rights reforms. She says the city balanced its budgets through a downturn without property-tax increases, layoffs, or furloughs.

Attorney general of Minnesota. His campaign says Minnesotans first elected him attorney general in 2018 and that he calls the job the people's lawyer. The site says the office has gone after insulin prices, opioid companies, scams, and medical debt. He says the office has lowered costs, including cutting the price of insulin, and has taken on price-gouging, medical debt, and opioid companies. He says he is protecting tenants, going after scammers, and standing up for student borrowers. He says he is challenging the Trump administration because no one is above the law, and that he is defending reproductive rights and access to gender-affirming care.

Ohio auditor of state running for attorney general. His campaign says he was elected auditor after more than two decades that included private-sector work and public office, and that he keeps a law practice in Celina. It says his audit team has pursued criminal cases against public officials and findings to recover taxpayer money. He says he would defend constitutional rights, including religious liberty, and challenge federal actions he argues exceed federal authority. He says he would fight the drug epidemic with treatment, prosecutions, and efforts to cut supply chains, and that he would work with police on human trafficking and survivor services. He says he would enforce consumer-protection laws against fraud, scams, and deceptive businesses, especially cases that target seniors, and he proposes a program to help patients challenge health-insurance denials.

U.S. representative running for another term. Keith Self's campaign says he is a native Texan, West Point graduate, and retired Army lieutenant colonel who served in the infantry and Special Forces. It says that after the Army he was Collin County judge and is seeking another term in Congress. He says he voted to restart border-wall construction, offered a bill to use seized cartel money on border security, and wants the federal government to repay Texas for its border spending. He says he cut the county property-tax rate, opposes stopgap federal budgets, and wants lower taxes, less spending, and energy permitting that expands American production. He says he started a caucus to stop what he calls the spread of Sharia law in Texas and the country.

Candidate for U.S. House in Colorado's 2nd District. Kelley Dennison says she is a Colorado native with roots in mountain towns and the Front Range, and a business owner. She says she is running so those communities have a voice in Congress on costs, energy, and the state's land and water. She says families are squeezed by housing, gas, inflation, and property taxes, and that the district should do better by veterans and seniors. She says parents should be partners in their children's education, and that responsible gun owners should not be punished for crimes committed by other people. She says she has signed a pledge to cosponsor and vote for a constitutional amendment limiting how long any person can serve in Congress.
District 1 · U.S. House · Rhode Island · Republican

Republican candidate and public-health worker running for Congress. Her campaign says she was born and raised in Boston, is a mother of three daughters, attended Boston Latin School and Suffolk University, and served in AmeriCorps. She says her career began at the nation's first community health center and grew into public-health operations. She says she would lower everyday costs and energy bills, offer tax relief for working families and seniors, and make housing more affordable. She says she would cut red tape for small businesses, expand workforce training, invest in community health centers, and support the ocean economy. She says she supports a parental bill of rights, curriculum transparency, school choice, stronger public safety, and secure borders.

New Hampshire's governor, running for another term. Kelly Ayotte is the state's 83rd governor. Her campaign says she previously served as attorney general and as a U.S. senator, and that she lives in Nashua. She says her first term sped up housing construction, fully funded child-care scholarships, and produced a balanced budget with no new taxes. She says she got cell phones out of classrooms, raised per-student school funding, and put more weight on reading. She says she rewrote bail rules, strengthened laws on domestic violence and trafficking, and used her veto on bills she calls hidden sales taxes.

Navy veteran and small-business CFO running for Georgia's 8th District. His campaign says he served from 1999 to 2002 as a nuclear operator on the USS Henry M. Jackson, and that he was the first Black nuclear operator on that boat during his service. He earned a PhD in public policy from Walden University and is chief financial officer of BroTagz Embroidery. He says he served on the Hapeville zoning board, as a legislative aide to State Senator Donzella James, and on the effort that created the city of South Fulton. He says education is a public good and he would fund affordable learning beyond K-12, including job skills for the district's health-care, retail, and manufacturing workers. He says he would strengthen Medicaid, Medicare, and VA care and fund rural clinics and hospitals, in a district he ties to Robins Air Force Base. He says he would seek federal money for roads, broadband, and utility upgrades, including solar and wind where communities want them, and back labor standards for workers.

Educator and consultant running for lieutenant governor. His campaign says he is a lifelong Oklahoman raised in Skiatook and Broken Arrow, the first in his family to graduate from college, and the holder of a doctorate in administration and leadership. It says he has taught and administered schools, owns Kelly B's Consulting, and serves on the board of Oklahoma City's family justice center. He says he would invest in small business, CareerTech, workforce training, and partnerships with Native nations, and would work on affordable housing and food insecurity. He says he would put more funding into public schools, respect teachers, and keep public dollars in public schools. He says he would expand health-care access in underserved places, promote tourism, and lead the office with public integrity rather than as a career politician.

Longtime manager of teams and operations Kelly Grappe says she spent decades leading teams, managing complex systems, and serving customers and businesses, and that she is not running because she has had a career in politics. She says she is running for secretary of state to take politics out of the office and make it work for the public. She says she will show how votes are cast, protected, counted, and verified, and answer doubts with facts rather than dismiss them. She says she will defend Arkansas's authority to run its own elections and oppose efforts to nationalize that work. She says transparency is one of the ways to build confidence that elections are secure.

Former Sarasota mayor and Democratic nominee for Florida's 16th District His campaign says he is a third-generation Floridian and a single father who grew up working his family's citrus stand near the Sarasota-Bradenton airport. He earned bachelor's and master's degrees from Georgetown, then spent four years in the Peace Corps in northern Guatemala. He later served as a Sarasota commissioner and mayor, built a nonprofit that helped first-generation students reach college without debt, and was a vice president at Eckerd College. He says he would lower insurance, health-care, and prescription costs, restore Medicare and Medicaid funding, and let the government negotiate drug prices. He says he would expand affordable housing and stop Wall Street from buying single-family homes. He says he would protect Tampa Bay, Sarasota Bay, and the coast by prohibiting offshore drilling and enforcing the Clean Water Act.

U.S. representative and OB-GYN. Kelly Morrison's campaign says she is a sixth-generation Minnesotan who practiced as an OB-GYN for more than 20 years and is the first pro-choice OB-GYN elected to Congress. She says she grew up and raised three children in the west metro, and that her husband John is an Army combat veteran. She says she is fighting health-care cuts she says would push Minnesotans off insurance and force hospitals to close, and that no one should go bankrupt to get care. She says she is working to exempt small businesses from tariffs and get them refunds, and to lower the costs of housing and child care. She says she takes no corporate PAC, federal-lobbyist, or dark-money money, supports a constitutional amendment to overturn Citizens United, and backs a ban on stock ownership by presidents, vice presidents, and members of Congress.

Mother, concrete-business owner, and nonprofit founder running for Congress. She says she is a mother of six and grandmother of 12, married to her high school sweetheart, with a business degree from the University of Central Florida. She co-owns a concrete contracting company serving northern Indiana and founded a nonprofit for at-risk youth. She says she would lower costs for housing, health care, education, utilities, and energy, and fight for Medicare for All. She says she would fully fund education from child care to college by taxing Wall Street, and put Hoosiers ahead of corporations and foreign governments. She says she would end U.S. wars in the Middle East and bring troops home, ban stock trading by Congress and the president, and release the Epstein files.

U.S. representative running in a newly drawn district. Ken Calvert's campaign says he is a lifelong Corona resident and a former small-business owner who now chairs the Defense Appropriations Subcommittee. It says that after Proposition 50 he is running in the 40th District, where Corona is the largest city. He says he wrote the law that created E-Verify and wants employers required to use it. He says he has secured more than a billion dollars for transportation, water, and clean-air projects in Riverside County. He says his office has helped veterans and seniors get benefits they are owed.

Information technology entrepreneur and Libertarian candidate for governor Ken Krawchuk's campaign says he has been a registered Libertarian since 1993 and is running for governor with John Thomas for lieutenant governor. The site says he was born in Philadelphia's Feltonville section and has lived in Abington for decades. He says he would veto tax increases, use the line-item veto, phase out the personal income tax, and abolish property taxes. He says he would end the state's monopoly on schooling and privatize public schools because too many students are behind in reading and math. His listed program also says he would eliminate parole for violent criminals, pardon nonviolent drug offenders, and decriminalize marijuana.

Candidate for the U.S. Senate. His campaign calls him a former attorney general who fought federal policies in court and is now running for the Senate. He says he will carry the president's agenda in Washington. He says he will push tax cuts, border security, deportations, an end to what he calls the weaponization of government, and less federal spending. He says he will take on large drug and food companies, seek more transparency in food and health care, and side with a Make America Healthy Again effort. He says he will defend gun rights and laws against abortion, oppose transgender participation in girls' sports, and support a clear legal framework for crypto, including the CLARITY Act.

Independent candidate for governor Kenneth Block is running for governor as an independent. His site says he wants the state government held accountable for waste, failed projects, and rising taxes. He says the state budget is about $15 billion and that residents are not getting services that match what they pay. He points to the Washington Bridge and large technology projects as examples of agencies repeating mistakes. He says his focus is accountability, fixing broken processes, and results for residents.

Third-generation Wyomingite and Vietnam veteran running for governor. He told Wyoming Public Media he was born in Cheyenne in 1950, that his family has worked in Wyoming for three generations, and that he ran a small business in Elk Mountain for 28 years. He does not have a campaign website. He says his first issue is free and open elections: a person should be able to file and run without having to join a party. He says health care is the main reason young people leave, and he wants a statewide system that connects rural clinics. He says he wants small business to grow, and he wants property tax ended for people once they turn 65.

Mechanical engineer running for Utah's 3rd District. He was born in Lehi, worked with mining, petroleum, geothermal, and solar industries, and says much of his career was spent on water, environmental cleanup, and teaching engineers. He says he is running because Washington has grown more divisive and disconnected, and he wants a representative who honors the Constitution. He calls for a moratorium on new data centers and says his priorities include Utah's land and water, Social Security, and the cost of health care. He says he takes no corporate PAC money and has pledged to limit his own term.

Marine veteran running for Congress. Kevin Burge's campaign says he is a Marine veteran with more than 20 years of leadership and deployments to Iraq and Afghanistan, and that he grew up without wealth in Los Alamos. It says his wife immigrated from Honduras, serves in the Texas Army National Guard, and their son attends public school in Tarrant County. He says he would fast-track affordable housing, crack down on corporate landlords, raise the minimum wage, and expand Medicaid. He says he supports Medicare for All, restoring abortion rights, tuition-free public college, and rules so data centers recycle water and limit pollution.

Candidate for U.S. Senate who says he was born on an Air Force base. His campaign says he earned an architectural drafting certificate in high school, used it to pay for an engineering degree, and later earned an MBA. It says that in office he has backed the Trump administration's agenda. He says he has backed bills to recognize groups of veterans and a constitutional amendment aimed at a balanced budget. He says he has voted to fund a border wall and to cut off federal money for sanctuary campuses, and that he wants small businesses to get capital. He says he would protect religious liberty, restrict abortion funding, and protect gun rights, including concealed-carry reciprocity.

Independent U.S. representative running for another term. Kevin Kiley's campaign says he grew up in the communities of the new 6th District, taught high school English, and prosecuted cases as a deputy attorney general before serving in the Assembly and winning a House seat in 2022. It says he chairs the subcommittee covering K-12 education and child care. He says he has worked across parties on measures to lower the cost of gasoline, groceries, utilities, and insurance. He points to a federal grant to ease traffic near Highways 65 and 80 and to a Lake Tahoe restoration law he says funds wildfire mitigation. He says he helped restore Medicare funding for senior programs and is focused on prosecuting violent crime and protecting children from fentanyl.

Former Stockton mayor and Marine veteran running for Congress. Kevin Lincoln's campaign says he was born in Stockton, raised in a military family, and joined the Marines in 2001, later serving on Marine One. It says he then managed a private-security district in Silicon Valley, became a Stockton pastor, and was elected mayor in 2019. He says he would secure the border, enforce immigration laws, and treat fentanyl trafficking as a threat to Valley families. He says he would cut wasteful spending and lower taxes as grocery, gas, and rent costs climb, pointing to budgets he balanced as mayor without a tax increase. He says he would oppose early release and shorter sentences for repeat offenders, and he highlights police pay and budget increases he backed as mayor.

Corporate controller running for Congress in Georgia's 6th District. He says he has spent 30 years as a controller, the person who audits the books, and that he is a fifth-generation native of Cobb County who has lived in the district his whole life. He says voters should be in charge of the people they elect. On schools, he wants federal education money returned to Georgia without federal strings, and he wants student aid and career programs to cover shorter technical training. On the budget, he says Congress should pass a budget through regular order, fund core obligations first, and make every other program justify another appropriation. He also says law enforcement should be funded, federal law should focus on people who have done something, there should be no national gun registry, and defense spending should start from readiness and replenishment rather than the size of the check.

Green Party candidate for lieutenant governor. He says he is the Green Party candidate and that the campaign will depend on voters telling other people, because he expects little corporate-media coverage. He says the lieutenant governor should judge bills by whether they protect health and a decent life for every Texan. He says his first bills would expand city bus fleets, invest in rural family-farm greenhouses and hemp, and change elections to ranked-choice voting, one statewide primary, and a nonpartisan redistricting commission. He says he would appraise property by rent or lease value instead of comparable sales and drop exemptions he calls special-interest favors. He says he favors a moratorium on data centers with strict limits on their electricity and water, and legal THC with rules to protect the public.

U.S. representative running for another term. Kevin Mullin's campaign says he was raised in South San Francisco, has lived on the Peninsula his whole life, and has been a local business owner and a D.J. It says he has served in local, state, and federal office and sits on the Energy and Commerce Committee. He says he would lower housing costs, send federal money to local child-care programs, and update the federal poverty line. He says he is defending medical research and the innovation economy in his district. His campaign also lists health-care costs, climate action, reproductive rights, and a fairer tax policy among his priorities.

Arkansas state senator and pastor Kim Hammer of Benton was elected to the state Senate in 2018 after eight years in the House, and he chairs the Senate Efficiency Committee. He has been pastor of Saline Missionary Baptist Church in Tull since 1978 and chaired the start of Saline Memorial Hospice. His campaign biography says that in the 94th General Assembly he sponsored bills to protect election integrity, including limits on electioneering near voting sites and authority for the legislature to look into voting irregularities. It says his priorities include making motor-vehicle registration and driver's-license renewal simpler. It says he was the lead sponsor of Act 403 of 2021, which lets the legislature end an executive order for a statewide public-health emergency.

Pediatrician and U.S. representative for Washington's 8th District. She chairs the Democratic Doctors Caucus and says travel around the district keeps turning up families squeezed by higher prices. She wrote a bill to suspend the federal gas tax for temporary relief, and she says she is fighting corporate price gouging, grocery mergers, and tariffs that hit farmers and small businesses. She is pushing housing bills, including a permanent housing-affordability proposal and support for the bipartisan Road to Housing package. She wants ACA premium tax credits restored and Republican Medicaid cuts undone so rural hospitals and Apple Health coverage stay in place.

Former prosecutor running for attorney general Kimberly Ahern's campaign says she was a prosecutor, advised two governors and three attorneys general, and worked as a regulator. It says she lives in Providence. She says that as attorney general she would put the criminal unit first and prosecute violent offenders, including murder, sexual assault, domestic violence, and trafficking. She says she would expand diversion so people with mental illness or addiction can get treatment while communities stay safe.
District 7 · U.S. House · North Carolina · Democratic

Social worker and professor running for Congress in North Carolina's 7th District. Her campaign says she is a mother, social worker, and professor who was raised by a Marine and a federal agent. She says she is running because policymakers have ignored hard-working neighbors in southeastern North Carolina. She says she would raise the federal minimum wage, close the overtime salary loophole, and end taxes on tips. She says she would protect Medicare and Medicaid, lower drug costs, and restore cancer-research funding. She says she would fund Head Start, Title I, and career education, and protect drinking water and coastal towns from flooding.

Former Hillsborough County commissioner and Democratic nominee for Florida's 12th District Her campaign says she is a mother, grandmother, and small-business owner who put herself through college, became a certified financial planner, and built an advisory firm. She served as a Hillsborough County commissioner from 2018 to 2022, including during the COVID-19 pandemic. She says she grew up in a working-class family that faced housing insecurity. She says she would fight for affordable housing, infrastructure, and fair wages because she knows what it is like to juggle bills and worry about rent. She says health care is a right and she would expand access, lower prescription costs, and defend reproductive care and mental-health services. She says she would fully fund public schools, raise teacher pay, and make sure veterans get the benefits and care they earned.

Kansas attorney general running for re-election. Kris Kobach's campaign site presents him as the sitting attorney general who filed for another term and highlights work with sheriffs and other law enforcement. The site points to prosecutions involving fentanyl trafficking and to a partnership with federal immigration enforcement that detained people with serious criminal records. It describes a multistate settlement with Meta that requires new safety features for children on Instagram and Facebook. It also describes a push to cut off phone numbers used for scam robocalls.

Arizona attorney general Kris Mayes is Arizona's attorney general. Her campaign calls her a consumer advocate and says she is the second woman, and the first mother, to serve as the state's chief law-enforcement officer and chief attorney. Her campaign says she took on Saudi-owned mega-farms over Arizona's water and corporations she says gouged people on rent and groceries. She says she has gone after drug smugglers, elder abusers, and scammers, and that her priorities include protecting rural groundwater, prosecuting sexual predators, and cracking down on AI that targets kids. Her priorities page also lists overturning tariffs, protecting $2.3 billion in Arizona tax dollars, and protecting Arizonans' freedoms.

U.S. representative for Michigan's 8th District. Her campaign says she grew up in a working-class Michigan town and later led Michigan Head Start, served as chief of staff at the state Department of Education, and was a vice president at the Skillman Foundation. She says her work has centered on child care and education. She says she has introduced bipartisan bills to lower grocery, housing, and medicine costs and to invest in child care, and that she led an effort to let families on SNAP buy hot prepared chicken. She says she worked to keep Saginaw's Social Security office open and opposes cuts to Social Security benefits. She says she wants to ban members of Congress from trading stock on insider information and to reverse Citizens United.

Muralist running for Congress in Tennessee's 1st District. Her campaign says she is a muralist and neighbor, not a career politician, who decided to run because the district's seat was not representing local people. She says corporate interests have been put ahead of human dignity. She says health care should be a right and that workers should be empowered. She says people should have the freedom to live with integrity, and that the campaign relies on grassroots donations rather than corporate PAC money.

Scientist running for Congress. Kristin Hook's campaign says she taught middle-school science through Teach For America, earned a PhD in animal behavior from Cornell, and did postdoctoral research in reproductive biology. It says she later left the lab for federal science and technology work. She says she would lower costs, fight corruption, and stop AI data centers from taking local water and electricity. She says billionaires should pay more, health care and public schools should be expanded, abortion rights restored, and the border secured.

Air Force veteran and nurse practitioner running for Congress in Ohio's 10th District. Kristina Knickerbocker says she is an Air Force veteran, an oncology nurse practitioner, and a mother of two who served as a major and nurse at Wright-Patterson Air Force Base. She says she put herself through school and followed her grandmother into nursing. She says she would ban congressional stock trading, end corporate PAC influence, pass term limits, protect voting rights, and close the lobbying revolving door. She also says she would cut taxes for working families, repeal tariffs that raise prices, build more housing, cap child-care costs, and make data-center companies pay for their own infrastructure.

Former Montana budget director and revenue director. His campaign says he was born in Great Falls, graduated from high school in Miles City, and has worked as a prosecutor, nonprofit leader, revenue director, and budget director. He lives in Billings and is running for the Senate. He says that as revenue director he led the largest income-tax rate cut in state history and put money back with taxpayers. He says that as budget director he helped cut spending and balance the budget. He says he is running to make life more affordable, keep communities safe, and protect what he calls the Montana way of life.

Incumbent · seeking a third term · former state senator Unopposed in the Democratic primary. His office’s public docket has leaned on consumer protection, workers, civil rights, guns, and reproductive rights. Capitol News Illinois counted roughly 90 legal fights with the Trump administration in the last two years. The office says those cases kept Illinois from losing access to more than $8 billion in federal funds. If reelected, keep lawyers on staff and rebuild capacity after lawmakers cut the office budget by $10 million this year. Says corruption has been a priority for eight years, including cases the office cannot announce because the U.S. attorney takes the public lead. Will keep defending state laws on abortion, guns, and civil rights, and joining multistate cases when federal policy hits Illinois funding.

U.S. representative for Maryland's 7th District, seeking another term. His campaign says he was born and raised in Baltimore, graduated with honors from Morgan State, and earned a master's degree at Johns Hopkins. It says he served on the city council and in Congress, led the NAACP, and returned to the House in 2020. The campaign says he still argues for bipartisan work on economic, education, and health-care issues. It highlights his role on the Americans with Disabilities Act, a ban on assault weapons, and the Henrietta Lacks law on diversity in cancer research. It also points to legislation that codified and increased funding for the Minority Business Development Agency.

Pharmacist, pharmacy owner, and farmer. His campaign says he was born and raised on Montana's Hi-Line, worked his family's farm, earned a Doctor of Pharmacy, and founded an independent pharmacy. He is running for the Senate as a Libertarian. He says he still owns his grandfather's farm and wants policy that deals with the stress on farmers and ranchers. He says he is a gun owner and hunter and wants Americans to keep unrestricted access to firearms. He says his work as a pharmacist showed him corruption and other problems in health care.

Business owner running for Congress. Kyle Kirkland's campaign says he arrived in California 40 years ago with $700 and went on to build businesses that created more than 1,000 jobs. It says he owns Club One Casino in Fresno, leads the California Gaming Association, and previously chaired Steinway Musical Instruments. He says housing, food, gas, and health care are too expensive because of over-regulation, and he would restart domestic production to bring costs down. He says government should be audited so tax dollars are not lost to waste and fraud. He says law enforcement needs tools against fentanyl and trafficking, and farmers need more water storage and fewer regulatory barriers.

Army Reserve officer running for Congress. Kyle Rable's campaign says he commissioned through Army ROTC at the University of Toledo, earned a master's while working in restaurants, and is a Texas Tech doctoral student and Army Reserve captain in Lubbock. It says he is running for workers and family farmers he argues both parties have forgotten. He says he would pass fair-pricing rules, limit corporate purchases of single-family homes, and offer tax credits for first-time buyers. He says he would fund child-care training and facilities, curb presidential tariff power, and bring back manufacturing jobs. He says legal paths to citizenship should expand because immigrants are part of West Texas communities.

District 14 · U.S. House · North Carolina · Democratic

Democratic nominee for Congress in North Carolina's 14th District. Her campaign says she is running to bring the experience of working families, entrepreneurs, and community leaders to Washington. She says her agenda comes from listening to families, workers, business owners, and faith leaders. She says health care is a necessity and that she would protect the Affordable Care Act, cap drug costs, and fund rural hospitals. She says she would raise the federal minimum wage, help small businesses get capital, and invest in affordable housing. She says she would put more federal money into public schools, apprenticeships, and student-debt relief, and demand oversight of federal spending.
District 10 · U.S. House · New Jersey · Democratic

U.S. representative for New Jersey's 10th District. Her campaign says she was born and raised in New Jersey, is a mother, and was the youngest woman elected to the Newark council, where she served as council president. It says she is the first Black woman to represent the 10th District and the youngest person New Jersey has elected to the House. She says she will not back down from attacks on women's rights or from a Justice Department prosecution she ties to her opposition to immigration enforcement. She says these are hard times and that she will keep protecting her community.

U.S. representative running for another term. Lance Gooden's campaign asks voters to send him back to Congress and says he has fought both the political swamp and calls for socialism. He says people are tired of Washington deal-making and of growing calls for socialism. He says another term would be used to protect what he calls God-given freedoms.

State's attorney for Fall River and Oglala Lakota counties Lance Russell's campaign says he is the longtime state's attorney for Fall River County and Oglala Lakota County and that he won the Republican nomination at the state party convention. The site describes him as a proponent of law and order. He says tough-on-crime policies work. He says his daily work is meant to protect the people of South Dakota.

Republican candidate for U.S. Senate. Larry Marker's campaign says that for nearly a decade, as a private citizen, he challenged political elites in New Mexico at personal cost. It says he is running to defend energy jobs, schools, and border security. He says he would defend oil and gas, including hydrogen and nuclear development, and oppose federal permitting delays that he says threaten school funding. He says the border is still a path for fentanyl and that he would back Border Patrol and local police. He says farmers and ranchers should not lose grazing, water, or working land to agency enforcement.

Governor of South Dakota Larry Rhoden's campaign says he is a fourth-generation South Dakotan and a rancher who served 16 years in the legislature and six years as lieutenant governor. It says he became governor and is running to stay in the office. He says his mission is to keep South Dakota strong, safe, and free, with less government and less red tape. He says his legislative record focused on low taxes, strong property rights, and personal freedom. He says he would stand up for law enforcement and for property rights, and keep the state open for business.

Businessman running for Congress in California's 32nd District. Larry Thompson's campaign describes him as a Catholic, a conservative, and an independent-minded Republican who has worked in business. He says he is running to bring together dissatisfied Democrats, conservatives, and no-party-preference voters. He says he will protect family values and wants people to use common sense and civility to find common ground. He says his goal is to get something done, and he asks for a vote in the November 3, 2026 general election.

Attorney and Democratic nominee for Florida's 4th District Her campaign says LaShonda "L.J." Holloway was named a Footsoldier for Justice by the Southern Christian Leadership Conference at 15, attended Howard University, and began a federal career at the Environmental Protection Agency. She graduated from Edward Waters University, earned a law degree at the University of Florida, worked on Capitol Hill for Representative Carrie Meek, and later led a mediation firm and community-lending work. She says she is a fourth-generation resident of the district. She says affordable health care should mean lower premiums and prescription costs, broader Medicare, and care that does not depend on a person's income. She says she would cut red tape and expand capital for small businesses, and make rent lower and homeownership more reachable for working families. She says Social Security should be protected and a full-time wage should cover food, housing, health care, and transportation.

U.S. representative running for another term. Lateefah Simon's campaign says she is a civil-rights advocate running for re-election in the 12th District, a vice chair of the Progressive and Equality caucuses, and the first Muslim woman elected to Congress from California. It says she was born blind, started organizing as a teenager, and lives in Oakland. Her campaign names public safety, affordable housing, homelessness, and job creation among her priorities. She also lists health care for all, reproductive freedom, immigration, disability rights, and LGBTQ rights. She highlights voting rights, climate, transportation, and what she calls a care economy.

U.S. representative running for another term. Laura Friedman's campaign says she served on the Glendale council and as mayor, then in the Assembly, before her election to Congress. It says her earlier work focused on climate, gun violence, reproductive freedom, LGBTQ rights, and housing. She says she is focused on affordable housing, universal health care and child care, and economic security for families. She says she has been a voice for public education, the environment, and safeguarding democracy. She says her legislative work expanded affordable housing and services for people with severe mental illness and people who are homeless.
District 4 · U.S. House · New York · Democratic

U.S. representative for New York's 4th District. Her campaign says she is a lawyer, a mother of four, and the former supervisor of the Town of Hempstead who grew up in Baldwin and is raising her family in Rockville Centre. It says she won the seat in 2024. She says she is committed to keeping families safe, growing the economy, and making Nassau County a place where people can afford a home or a business. She says her first term has focused on working across the aisle to lower the cost of living and bring federal investment back to the county.

Small-business owner running for Congress. Laura Jones's campaign says she is a lifelong Texan, an Army mom, a small-business owner, and a working-class candidate running in 2026. She says the minimum wage should rise and be tied to the cost of living so a full-time worker can cover housing, utilities, and food. She supports Medicare for All, including cutting out insurance middlemen and negotiating drug and medical prices. She says taxes should fall for most households and rise for billionaires and large corporations.

U.S. representative running for another term. Laurel Lee's campaign says she serves on the Judiciary, Energy and Commerce, and House Administration committees. It says she was an impeachment manager in the Mayorkas case and served on the task force on the attempt on President Trump's life and the House artificial-intelligence task force. The site says that under President Trump she is focused on turning conservative priorities into results for the 15th District. It quotes his endorsement of her on the border, innovation, the military and veterans, and the Second Amendment.

U.S. representative running for Colorado's 4th District. Lauren Boebert's campaign says she serves in the U.S. House and is running to represent the 4th District. It says she is the mother of four boys and, before Congress, volunteered with women in the Garfield County Jail and helped gather signatures against the National Popular Vote Compact. She says she believes in personal freedom, the rights of citizens, and the Constitution. She says she has passed House bills on energy production and water rights, and has pushed back on federal land rules she says hurt ranchers and farmers. She says a jobs bill she got signed in 2023 will create 1,000 jobs in southern Colorado.

Special-education teacher running for Congress in Louisiana's 1st District. She says she has spent 17 years beside Louisiana students, families, and educators and is a nationally board-certified special education teacher and union member. She says she is running because people who teach, care for neighbors, and build communities need someone who will fight as hard as they do. She says Louisiana families are squeezed by unaffordable insurance, health-care costs, underfunded schools, and an economy that leaves too many people behind. Her campaign says the district needs lower costs, strong schools and hospitals, safe communities, and a representative who fights for working people. She says she wants to advocate for environmental, constitutional, economic, and health protections in a region she calls overlooked.

Republican nominee who says she is a trafficking survivor and a mother of six. Her campaign says Lauren B. Peña grew up in Austin, survived human trafficking, and rebuilt her life through faith and family. It calls her a constitutional conservative and a longtime Austin resident running for the 37th District. She says she would audit agencies, expose fraud, cut federal spending she ties to inflation, and cut regulations she says are raising energy costs. She says she would defend parental rights and school choice, restore law-enforcement funding, and make veterans' care a priority. She says her first bill would be the SAFE NIGHTS Act to fight human trafficking, and that she would press to release the Epstein files.

Candidate for governor of Tennessee. She says she is a seventh-generation Tennessean who has started businesses with survivors of human trafficking, studied workforce gaps, led nonprofits, and advised organizations. She says she is running because she does not believe a person must be a political extremist to be represented. She says she would eliminate the grocery tax, cap property taxes, and make it possible to own a home. On schools, she says she would end vouchers, reduce testing, limit screens, and add 50,000 child-care slots. She says she would close health-care deserts, challenge middlemen who raise costs, and allow no new data centers until the state sets the rules.

Attorney and former Social Security Administration adviser running for Congress. Lauren Reinhold's site says she has been a Kansan for 32 years and an attorney for 28, including more than 25 years in public institutions as an attorney adviser at the Social Security Administration. She says she resigned after cuts at the agency and is running to defend working families and rural communities in the Big First. She says rural hospitals are the lifeblood of their communities and pledges to rebuild rural health care. She says farm policy should put producers, family operations, and main-street businesses ahead of corporate monopolies. She calls Social Security a hard-earned promise and says she will fight underfunding and political interference that delay benefits.

Libertarian nominee for Indiana secretary of state. Lauri Shillings's site says she is a creative director at the University of Indianapolis, has owned a small business since 2000, chairs the Hamilton County Libertarian Party, and holds a degree in community and nonprofit leadership. She says she is running to restore trust in elections and to keep the office from being used as a party tool. She wants simpler, reliable online services for business filings and records. She says government systems should be efficient and that voters should have clear guides for registration and voting.
District 1 · U.S. House · North Carolina · Republican

Retired Army colonel running for Congress in North Carolina's 1st District. She says she is a combat commander and business leader, an Iraq War veteran who led troops in combat, and that she lives in Edenton with her husband, a fellow Army veteran. She says she is running because career politicians are making life harder for working families in eastern North Carolina. She says she will fight to cut taxes and lower health-care and living costs so families can get ahead. She says border security is national security and that Border Patrol agents need the resources to keep dangerous drugs out of the country. She says she grew up on a farm and will cut regulations on farmers, fishermen, and the seafood industry, defend the Second Amendment, and invest in a ready military.

Retired defense intelligence officer running for Congress The campaign says Lee McInnis is an Alabama native who served six years in Army intelligence and then 28 years in the defense intelligence community, including as acting director of intelligence for a NATO and U.S. special operations task force in Afghanistan. After federal service he taught communications and American government and earned a master's degree in history from Auburn. He says the economy favors the very wealthy and that he wants working families to keep more of what they earn. He says the 3rd District has counties without hospitals, pediatricians, or labor-and-delivery care, and that health care should be available to everyone. He says he will not take money from corporate PACs or PACs tied to foreign governments, and that he will hold town halls.

Retired Army brigadier general and Democratic nominee for Florida's 13th District Her campaign says she is a retired Army brigadier general, a third-generation veteran, a lawyer, and a mother who put herself through college, including with Army ROTC at Elon. She served about 30 years, including work at the State Department and as an advisor to Army Cyber Command, and later helped veterans get health care. She and her husband have lived in the Tampa Bay area for more than 20 years and raised their daughter there. She says neighbors cannot keep up with the cost of housing, health care, insurance, food, and fuel, and that is why she is running. She says she would ban stock trading by officials in Washington, bar former members of Congress from corporate lobbying, and set term limits. She says she would protect the beaches and the coastal economy, and keep the promise of care for veterans and military families.

Community advocate running for Congress. Leticia Gutierrez's campaign says she has lived in the district for 45 years, is the daughter of farm laborers, and earned a finance degree from the University of St. Thomas. It says she is a military mother who became a children's-health advocate after her son developed asthma. She says her priorities are lower costs, good jobs, strong public schools, affordable health care, and secure retirements. She says she is for industry and jobs without blank checks for billionaires, and for safe neighborhoods, secure borders, and equal justice. She says she opposes wars of choice and corporate handouts, and wants government to answer to families rather than the highest bidder.

Attorney general of New York since 2019, seeking another term. Her campaign says she has used the office to lower costs for working families, hold powerful interests accountable, and protect New Yorkers' rights and safety. It says that work has included suits against the Trump administration over rights and funding for health care, public schools, and jobs. The site lists public safety, jobs and affordability, consumer protection, and health care as her priorities. She says the office should keep challenging powerful interests that she argues are trying to control government. She ties that work to protecting funding for health care, public education, and jobs.

District 2 · U.S. House · New Hampshire · Republican

Republican nominee for New Hampshire's 2nd District. Her campaign says she was born to poor working-class parents in Sichuan and grew up during Mao's Cultural Revolution before coming to the United States. She says she has been married for 34 years, has three adult children, and manages rental properties while speaking about socialism and communism. She says she has signed a pledge to cosponsor and vote for a term-limits amendment of three House terms and two Senate terms. Her good-government plan calls for single-subject bills, on-time budgets, a ban on stock trading by members and their immediate families, a balanced-budget amendment, and an end to earmarks. On prices she says special interests and the federal government should get out of managing the economy, energy should include nuclear, oil, solar, coal, and wind, and spending should come down so the debt can be paid down.

U.S. representative running for another term. Linda Sánchez's campaign says she was born in Orange County to Mexican immigrant parents, a mechanic and a teacher, and earned degrees from UC Berkeley and UCLA's law school. It says she is the first woman from the electrical workers' union elected to Congress and a co-founder of the Labor Caucus. She says she is fighting to lower costs for working families and to protect her community from the Trump administration and ICE. She says she wants safe, quality education for children and job growth through innovation and manufacturing. She says workers deserve safe jobs, good wages, and a dignified retirement.

Democratic candidate running for Louisiana's 6th District. She says she grew up stretching a dollar and waiting on doctors, and that she has worked in public schools, served in federal programs, stood with families in crisis, and studied the law. She says she is not a career politician. She says she would make daily life more affordable, protect Social Security, Medicare, and Medicaid, lower prescription costs, and raise wages. She says she would bring federal money home for I-10 and I-12, bridges, drainage, flood protection, and affordable flood insurance. She says she would fight violent crime, trafficking, and fentanyl while supporting voting rights, civil rights, and due process.

Chaplain and Iowa state representative running for Congress. She says public service began as a chaplain beside people in their hardest hours, and that as a state representative she has argued government should serve people rather than the powerful. She is running to level the playing field for Iowans who are choosing between rent, food, medicine, and care for family. She says no one should go bankrupt or ration medicine because of a medical emergency, and that rural health care needs urgent changes as cancer rates rise. She says money in politics has fueled partisanship, and that getting money out of politics is necessary for a healthier system. She says Iowa farmers cannot wait another decade for a farm bill, and she opposes private-school vouchers she says benefit the most fortunate.

Speaker of the Minnesota House. Her campaign says she was elected to the Minnesota House in 2018, served on the ROCORI School Board, and ran a small business before that. In 2025 she became Speaker, and the site says she was the first Black lawmaker and the first Republican woman in that post. She says her first priority as governor would be helping families afford their lives, including lower income-tax brackets, lower car-tab fees, and an end to the state tax on Social Security benefits. She says she would create a nonpartisan inspector general to look for fraud in state programs before money leaves the door. She says she would back police, firefighters, and other first responders.

Former Wyoming state senator running for Congress. Her campaign says she was born and raised in Laramie, earned degrees from the University of Wyoming and the University of Oregon and a law degree from Wyoming, and served in the State Senate from Laramie for ten years, from 1985 to 1995, including as minority floor leader. She says she has directed the Albany County Library, practiced law, and worked more than twenty years as a financial advisor. She says public lands should stay public, and she would work with local communities to keep access open rather than sell or transfer the land. She says she would restore Affordable Care Act subsidies, keep the rural-hospital funding she says is set to end, and work toward health coverage for everyone. She says she would cut tariffs, raise taxes on the wealthy, lower taxes for people making under $100,000, and help first-time buyers and renters with housing.

U.S. representative and former financial-services executive. Her campaign says she grew up in Stockbridge, worked through high school and college, and earned a business degree from Northwood University. She says she spent 30 years in the private sector, including American Express and Hantz Financial, and lives in Romeo with her husband Mike and their four children. She says she would cut taxes and regulations on small business and support trade deals that help Michigan farmers and workers. She says she would build a border wall, enforce immigration law, and defend the Second Amendment for law-abiding owners. She says health coverage should be sold across state lines with wider use of health savings accounts, and she opposes taxpayer funding of abortion.

U.S. representative running for another term. Lizzie Fletcher's campaign says she is a Houston native who practiced business litigation at Vinson & Elkins and became the first woman partner at the firm AZA. It says she was first elected in 2018 and serves on Energy and Commerce, where she works on energy and health care. She says the district's values are inclusion, innovation, and collaboration, and that those should produce progress and opportunity. She says she looks for common-sense solutions for Houstonians rather than slogans, including on energy and health policy.

U.S. representative for Pennsylvania's 11th District. Lloyd Smucker owned the Smucker Company for 25 years, served in the state Senate as education committee chair, and was elected to Congress in 2016. His campaign highlights taxes, retirement, health care costs, energy, small business, and family farms. He says he wants to cut taxes, protect retirement, and spend taxpayer dollars more carefully. He also lists lower health care costs, American energy, and support for small businesses and family farms.

U.S. representative for Florida's 23rd District Her campaign says she has represented Palm Beach County in Congress since 2013, after 14 years in the Florida Legislature, including as the first Democratic woman to serve as minority leader, and eight years as mayor of West Palm Beach. She serves on the Appropriations Committee and is the lead Democrat on its national-security subcommittee. She founded the Democratic Women's Caucus and is the mother of a Marine veteran. She says she is fighting cuts to health care, Social Security, Medicare, and Medicaid, and working to lower costs for families. She says she works to protect the environment and expand access to housing. She says she is an advocate for women's reproductive freedom.

Attorney running for attorney general. She says she never planned to run, and that she has practiced at a large New York firm, at Micron Technology, and for clients in Idaho. She says earlier attorneys general such as Jim Jones, Larry EchoHawk, and Lawrence Wasden kept the office on the law rather than on politics. She says she will give state agencies and the Land Board legal advice based on the law, and hire for ethics and skill rather than ideology. She says she will issue prompt opinions for legislators and state officials and follow the statute even when that is politically inconvenient. She says she will oppose selling federal public lands in Idaho or closing them to the public.

U.S. representative and working mother from Lowell. She says she was born and raised in a working-class family in Lowell, is the mother of two girls, and has about 25 years of experience in Congress and the private sector. She says she is an optimist who will work with both parties. She says health care is a right, that she would strengthen the Affordable Care Act, and that Medicare should be able to negotiate drug prices. She says she would invest in education from early childhood through apprenticeships and fight student debt. She says she supports a constitutional amendment to overturn Citizens United and a pathway to citizenship alongside updated border security.

U.S. representative and former state legislator running for another term. Lou Correa's campaign says he was raised by working-class parents and has focused since 1998 on helping Orange County families reach the middle class. It says he served in the Assembly, the state Senate, and as an Orange County supervisor before Congress. He says public service should be about people rather than partisan games. He says he wants practical results for a blue-collar district he describes as home to many veterans and Dreamers.

U.S. representative for Georgia's 6th District. She says the title that matters most is mom. After her son Jordan Davis was shot and killed in 2012, she left a 30-year career at Delta Air Lines, worked with Everytown for Gun Safety and Moms Demand Action, and then ran for the seat once held by Newt Gingrich. She highlights House passage of universal background checks and red-flag laws, and she says her work in Congress is aimed at laws that help children and families. A two-time breast cancer survivor, she says communities need affordable care, including cancer screening, contraceptives, and family-planning services, and she opposed defunding Planned Parenthood. She supports the Equality Act to bar LGBTQ discrimination in work, housing, and credit, and she points to federal infrastructure spending for safe water, high-speed internet, and a cleaner environment.

Former mayor of Hartford running for Congress The campaign says Luke Bronin was mayor of Hartford from 2016 to 2024, where he worked to pull the city back from bankruptcy, add housing, and create the Hartford Youth Service Corps. He says he is running because families are struggling while billionaires get tax breaks. He says he will focus on bringing down costs for housing, health care, groceries, childcare, and elder care. He wants Medicare and Medicaid protected and a push toward universal health care. He says he would abolish ICE, build more housing, and safeguard reproductive freedom.

Engineer and U.S. representative running for another term. Luz Rivas's campaign says she grew up in Pacoima with a single mother who had immigrated from Mexico, then earned an electrical-engineering degree from MIT and a master's in education from Harvard. It says she worked at Motorola, founded a girls' science nonprofit, served six years in the Assembly, and was elected to the House in 2025. She says her Assembly priority was funding for infrastructure, education, and health care in the Valley, along with environmental justice. She says she worked to expand computer-science and climate education across California. Her campaign says that in her first House term she joined Democratic leadership and co-chairs a bipartisan STEM education caucus.

Libertarian candidate for the U.S. Senate. Her campaign says she is from Ironwood in the Upper Peninsula, with a background in computer science, and that she built the campaign herself without PAC money. She says Michigan needs a senator who answers to residents rather than a political machine. She says she would protect the Great Lakes and push affordable health care, including Medicaid for all. She calls for fair wages, green jobs, and support for small businesses, and for social, racial, and LGBTQIA+ equity. She says she would defend voting rights and constitutional freedoms, and that she is not beholden to party bosses or corporate donors.

Former teacher running for governor. Her campaign says she is a lifelong Nebraskan, a former teacher, a mother, and a faith leader. She says she is running to bring what she calls common sense, compassion, and integrity back to the governor's office. She says she wants low taxes, strong schools, and an economy where people can get ahead. She says leaders should follow votes the public has already cast, including on medical marijuana, paid sick leave, the minimum wage, and school vouchers. She says she would push for a government that tells people what they need to know, not only what they want to hear.

Sacramento City Council member running for Congress. Mai Vang's campaign says she is the daughter of Hmong refugees, the oldest of 16 children, and the first in her family to attend college. It says she has been a teacher, a school board member, and a Sacramento City Council member focused on neighborhoods the city had overlooked. She says she takes no corporate PAC money and would raise the minimum wage with inflation, tax billionaires, and pass the PRO Act. She says she would fight for Medicare for All, an end to medical debt, and federal protection of reproductive care. She says she would fund more affordable housing, stop corporations from buying up single-family homes, and pause new data centers so households do not pay their power costs.
District 5 · U.S. House · South Carolina · Democratic

Campaign manager and candidate who says she puts people over party. She says she will fight for practical solutions through conversation and collaboration, and that she will not bend her values to party or special interests. Former state representative running for U.S. House in Colorado's 8th District. He says he has been an economist for the Army Corps of Engineers, a lawyer, and a state representative from Adams County. He says he would expand tax credits for working parents, close corporate tax loopholes, and bring down the cost of drugs, insurance premiums, and energy bills. He says he will protect Social Security and Medicare from benefit cuts and a higher retirement age, and cap insulin at $35 a month. He says his campaign takes no corporate PAC money, and that he would ban members of Congress from trading stocks and push to undo Citizens United.

Council to make neighborhoods safer.

U.S. representative for Ohio's 9th District. She says she would fully fund Medicare and Medicaid, restore Affordable Care Act tax credits, and lower prescription prices and the cost of child care and long-term care.

State representative, 12th District, since 2021 · chairs Financial Institutions Chicago. Previously deputy chief of staff at the Department of Commerce and Economic Opportunity. Keep withholding pay from contractors who violate the Prevailing Wage Act. Change the Vendor Payment Program so finance firms cannot cherry-pick the receivables of larger vendors. U.S. representative for Florida's 27th District Her campaign says she was born in Miami's Little Havana to Cuban parents who fled after Fidel Castro took power. She graduated from the University of Miami and from Harvard, which she says she paid for herself, then anchored CNN en Español, covered the White House and wars in the Gulf and El Salvador, and interviewed Fidel Castro. She says she is funding Everglades restoration, coastal flood protection, and cleaner water in Biscayne Bay. She says she opposes socialism and communism, has pushed sanctions on the governments of Cuba, Venezuela, and Nicaragua, and supports term limits.

Attorney and former city council member running for Congress in Ohio's 14th District. Maria Jukic says she is a licensed attorney, a former Euclid councilwoman, and the child of immigrants from a union family, and that she worked in health care for 24 years. She says she is running for people in the political middle who are doing everything right and still falling behind. She says she will defend the Constitution and the rule of law, and that she is looking for practical answers to a health system in which many people lack insurance or carry medical debt. She says she will stand up for workers and regular people and look for common ground instead of sorting the country into two extremes.

Louisville trauma nurse and small-business owner running for Congress. Born in Cuba, she says she arrived in the United States at 21 after an 11-year asylum process, became a citizen, built a small business, and later earned a nursing degree as a single mother of two. She says she is running to defend freedoms she once lived without. She says she believes in free enterprise, safe communities, legal immigration, and constitutional rights. Her campaign lists defending capitalism, a safer Louisville, lower taxes, and protecting the unborn among her priorities. She also lists protecting women's sports.

Doctor, Army veteran, and U.S. representative running for re-election. She says she is the fourth of eight children, left home at 16 for community college, and enlisted in the Army at 18, rising from private to lieutenant colonel over 24 years. She later practiced medicine in Ottumwa, served in the Iowa Senate, and was elected to Congress in 2020. She says she is running for re-election because Iowans deserve someone who will keep fighting for them and for Iowa values. On her 2026 tour she says she is fighting for lower health-care costs, lower taxes, and common sense.

U.S. representative and auto-shop owner from southwest Washington. She describes herself as a fifth-generation Washingtonian, a pro-choice mother, and a trades small-business owner who built a house by hand and brought her child to work because day care was too expensive. She says she will oppose a national abortion ban and protect the freedom to see a doctor. She wants local police and firefighters paid enough to stay, and she is pushing a right to repair so farmers and customers are not forced back to the manufacturer. She says the campaign takes no corporate PAC money and is working to lower housing, child care, and health-care costs.

U.S. representative working on family costs, health care, and military families. She says she is a proud Army brat representing service members, veterans, and military families, and that her time in Congress has centered on costs, jobs, and care. She says working people and small businesses need lower costs, more jobs, and an economy put back on track. She wants health care people can afford, Medicare protected, and more renewable energy. She says she has led bipartisan work on food insecurity and housing for military families in a district she describes as full of service members and veterans.

U.S. representative for Florida's 26th District His campaign says he was born and raised in Florida, spent 14 years in the Florida Legislature, and was the youngest person elected to the Florida Senate, at 31. He is in his eleventh term in the U.S. House, vice chair of the Appropriations Committee, and founder of the bipartisan Everglades Caucus. He says he would end the tax on tips and overtime and make working-family tax cuts permanent. He says he would detain and remove people here illegally who have committed crimes, and crack down on fentanyl trafficking. He says he would continue Everglades restoration and fund school-violence prevention and parental rights in education.

U.S. representative campaigning as a conservative voice for rural Missouri. He tells voters he spent more than 23 years as a local television anchor before taking that platform to Congress. He says he is fully opposed to abortion and will defend what he calls a right to life for the unborn. He wants federal spending, waste, and fraud cut back in order to slow the national debt. He says he will defend the Second Amendment for law-abiding owners and will oppose efforts to reduce police funding.

Colorado state senator and Republican nominee for U.S. Senate. Mark Baisley says he is an aerospace engineer who leads a Colorado software company and has served in the state House and the state Senate. He says he is the Republican nominee for the U.S. Senate in 2026. He says that in the legislature he worked on jobs, education, and essential services while limiting government intrusion into private life. He says he has defended water rights, protected the energy industry, and opposed reckless spending and government overreach. He says he will take that approach to Washington, with an emphasis on liberty and Colorado families.

U.S. representative running for another term. Mark DeSaulnier's campaign says he drove trucks, waited tables, and ran Bay Area restaurants before serving on the Concord council, as county supervisor, and in the Legislature. It says he has represented an East Bay House district, sits on Transportation and Infrastructure, and is the top Democrat on Ethics. He says workers need a voice as artificial intelligence changes jobs, and he points to proposals on layoffs, CEO pay, and the right to organize. He says housing, transit, and wages have to be tackled together so families are not pushed out of the Bay Area, and he highlights clean-air rules and a national electric-vehicle charging program. He says he would protect cancer-research funding, codify abortion and contraception access, and pursue immigration enforcement that does not separate families.

Candidate for South Carolina secretary of state. His campaign says South Carolina businesses are growing and that the secretary of state's office has made filings easier. District 8 · U.S. House · North Carolina · Republican

Pastor and U.S. representative for North Carolina's 8th District. His campaign says he was born and raised in Winston-Salem, the youngest of five children, and is a husband, father, and pastor. He says he would fortify the border, enforce immigration law, and keep a strong military that honors veterans. He says parents, not Washington, should choose public, private, charter, or home schools, and he wants to cut spending that he says drove inflation.

Retired Pinal County sheriff running for Congress in Arizona's 5th District. His campaign says he is not a career politician. It says he spent eight years as sheriff protecting Arizona communities, confronting cartels, and fighting human trafficking. He says he will secure the border, stop the cartels, and restore order to immigration while protecting legal immigration and commerce. He says he will defend the Constitution, support law enforcement, and stand with families and small businesses. He says he wants lower costs, protection for taxpayers, and stronger American jobs.

Small-business owner and U.S. representative from southern Indiana. A lifelong Hoosier from the Jasper area, he says he and his wife Kim have been married 40 years and have four children. He says less government creates more jobs, and that in the state legislature he fought for economic growth, individual liberties, and constitutional values. He says voters should know he is a Hoosier businessman and a Christian who will stand up to what he calls the woke mob in Washington. He says he is a pro-Trump conservative and will keep fighting for the values he learned growing up in Jasper. He says faith, family, and hard work are what make communities strong, and that he wants those communities more prosperous.

Educator and former council member running for Congress. Mark Nair's campaign says he is a husband, father, inventor, and former Amarillo city council member who has lived in the district for more than 30 years. It says he taught at Amarillo College, led innovation at a local employer, and holds patents. He says tariffs should be set by Congress rather than a president, and that he wants wages people can live on. He says government should stop using artificial intelligence for facial recognition and social-media surveillance until privacy rules exist, and that workers should know when AI affects their jobs. He says health care should put people ahead of insurers and corporate profits.

U.S. representative and former Wisconsin state legislator. He says his politics started in blue-collar Kenosha, where at age eight he delivered literature for his father, a city alderman. He took 14 years in the Assembly to Congress in 2013 and co-chairs the LGBT Equality Caucus and the Labor Caucus. He says he uses private-sector and public-sector experience to promote job growth and support families in south-central Wisconsin. He is chair emeritus of the Congressional Progressive Caucus and describes himself as a progressive leader. A campaign news note says he stopped taking corporate PAC money for his reelection.

U.S. representative and former teacher running for another term. Mark Takano's campaign says he was born and raised in Riverside, taught high school, and served on a community-college board before Congress. It says his parents and grandparents were sent to Japanese American incarceration camps during World War II, and that in 2012 he became the first openly gay person of color elected to Congress. He says that as a teacher and trustee he worked on public education and job training for adults. His campaign says he is the ranking Democrat on the House Veterans' Affairs Committee and also serves on Education and the Workforce.

Businessman and former state representative running for Congress. His campaign says he is a Christian husband, father, and grandfather who spent more than 30 years building insurance and construction businesses in Tulsa. It says that in the state House he helped pass a large tax cut, immigration enforcement, and a homeowner bill of rights. He says he would lower costs for working families by cutting inflationary spending, red tape, and energy and regulatory costs, and by restoring fiscal discipline. He says every nation has a right to secure its borders, enforce its laws, and put its citizens first. He says he is running to help build an economy that works for the people who fund it and to bring good jobs back.

Former major-league player running for Congress. Mark Teixeira's campaign says he is a Christian husband and father and a former All-Star whose father was a Navy veteran and whose mother was a teacher. It says five seasons with the Texas Rangers tied him to the state, and that he moved back in 2021. He says he would secure the border, deport people here illegally, and go after cartels. He says he would cut federal spending, expand oil, gas, and nuclear production, and defend parental rights, the Second Amendment, and the unborn.

U.S. senator whose campaign says he helped write the Affordable Care Act and a bipartisan infrastructure law. It says he is the top Democrat on the Senate Intelligence Committee and has worked with both parties on bills signed into law. He wants more housing through rehabilitation and faster permits, and an easier path to a first mortgage, and he says lower health costs depend on a basic standard of care for every American. He says companies that profit from artificial intelligence should help prepare workers and pay for the energy that technology will demand. He supports an assault-weapons ban and background checks, and he says Virginia voters should be able to put abortion access, marriage equality, and restoration of voting rights into the state constitution.

Farmer, business owner, and U.S. representative from Howe, Indiana. He and his wife Christy still farm at Schonbrook Farm and own businesses including a farm-to-fork restaurant. He says Washington's debt and spending, which he puts at $37 trillion, are the biggest threat to the American dream, and that waste should be cut without raising taxes. He says a repaired tax system should let workers keep more of what they earn, and that Social Security and Medicare can be preserved alongside entitlement reforms that reduce the debt. He says he wants to finish a border wall and strengthen national security.

Attorney and former prosecutor running for Congress. Marni von Wilpert's campaign says she is a workers'-rights attorney from the Obama years and a former prosecutor. It says she has gone after wage theft, opioid companies, and chemical polluters, launched first-time homebuyer grants, and defended abortion rights. She says she is running to lower costs for working families and to clean up corruption in Washington. She says that as the daughter of an immigrant Army veteran she is fighting ICE tactics she calls unconstitutional, including masked agents. She says she wants a secure border and a path to citizenship for long-term residents and Dreamers.

Iowa Colony council member running for Congress. Marquette Greene-Scott's campaign says she is mayor pro tem of Iowa Colony, the youngest of five children of a Vietnam veteran, and the mother of an adult daughter. It says she moved to Texas in 2010 as a single mother and recently married. She says she is running because Congress is broken and she will judge issues by what is best for the district rather than by party. She says her focus is creating jobs, improving infrastructure, and protecting essential rights.
Candidate for the U.S. Senate. Her campaign site calls her a champion for Tennessee and says the campaign is powered by ordinary people. No 2026 issue list was found for this candidate.

Candidate for governor of Tennessee. Her campaign says that, as a member of the Tennessee Senate, she led the fight against a state income tax. She says she will keep taxes and prices low and cut spending and regulation she calls unnecessary so more companies move to Tennessee. She says she will help Tennessee-grown small businesses expand at home while the state recruits outside employers. She says she will work with businesses on workforce gaps, including training, and commit to filling them.

Minister running for Congress. She says she would cut federal spending, back Texas oil and gas, and support Border Patrol against illegal crossings and trafficking.

Former attorney general running for Congress in South Dakota. Republican candidate for Nevada's 3rd District.
